learn.hook: Why does the Moon never crash into the Earth? Spotting a pattern and asking 'why' led to the answer!
points: Mathematics is the search for patterns, and for explanations of why those patterns happen.
Maths is both an art and a science: it has beautiful patterns to create and enjoy, and exact rules that help us understand the world.
Watching the regular motion of planets led to the idea of gravitation, which today helps us launch satellites.
Finding patterns in genomes (the 'instructions' inside living cells) helps doctors understand and treat diseases.
Maths helps in daily life (shopping, cooking, time-tables) and in big things too: science, economics, counting votes in a democracy, building houses and bridges, and making phones and computers.

example.q: Ritu notices that the Sun rises a little earlier every day from January to June. What would a mathematician do next?
steps: First, describe the pattern clearly: sunrise time keeps getting earlier.
Next, collect data (note the time each day) to check it really happens.
Then ask WHY it happens, and look for an explanation (the Earth's tilt as it goes round the Sun).
example.answer: Describe the pattern, check it with data, then search for why it happens.

learn.reallife: Railway time-tables, cricket run rates, election vote counts, weather forecasts and the GPS in a phone all use mathematics.

games.title: Maths true or false
items: Mathematics is only about doing sums quickly.
It is the search for patterns and the reasons behind them.
Maths can be called both an art and a science.
It has beauty and creativity, and also exact rules.
Patterns in planet motion helped people understand gravitation.
The regular orbits led to the theory of gravitation.
A shopkeeper giving change uses no maths.
Giving change is subtraction.
Explaining WHY a pattern happens is part of mathematics.
Maths looks for explanations, not just patterns.
Computers and mobile phones are built without any mathematics.
All technology is built using mathematics.

quiz.q: Which sentence best describes mathematics?
options: The search for patterns and why they happen
quiz.explain: Mathematics looks for patterns and explains why they happen. Tables and counting are just small parts of it.
steps: Key idea: maths is the search for patterns and for the reasons why they happen.
Tables, counting money and neat drawings are only small parts or not maths at all.
So the answer is 'The search for patterns and why they happen'.
Answer: The search for patterns and why they happen
quiz.mistake: Thinks maths is only memorising or calculating

quiz.q: Why do we say maths is both an art and a science?
options: Because it is taught in art class
Because it has beautiful patterns and also exact rules that explain the world
quiz.explain: Maths creates beautiful patterns (art) and gives exact tools to understand nature (science).
steps: Art side: maths creates beautiful patterns.
Science side: maths gives exact rules that explain the world.
It is not about paint or art class.
So maths is both an art and a science because of beautiful patterns and exact rules.
Answer: Because it has beautiful patterns and also exact rules that explain the world
quiz.mistake: Takes 'art' to mean drawing or painting only

quiz.q: Studying the regular movement of planets led scientists to which idea?
quiz.explain: The patterns in planet motion were explained by gravitation, and that understanding is used to launch satellites.
steps: Planets move in regular patterns in the sky.
Explaining these patterns led to the theory of gravitation.
This idea is used today to launch satellites.
So the answer is 'The theory of gravitation'.
quiz.mistake: Does not link planetary motion with gravitation

quiz.q: How do patterns in the genome help people?
options: They help doctors understand and treat diseases
quiz.explain: A genome holds the instructions of a living thing. Finding patterns in it helps medicine.
steps: A genome holds the instructions of a living thing.
Finding patterns in it helps us understand how the body works.
That helps doctors understand and treat diseases.
Bread, rivers and cricket have nothing to do with genomes.
Answer: They help doctors understand and treat diseases
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a genome is

quiz.q: Which of these everyday jobs uses maths?
quiz.explain: Sharing 12 laddoos among 4 friends is division: 3 each.
steps: Look for a job that needs numbers.
Sharing 12 laddoos among 4 friends needs division: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 each.
Smelling, listening and sleeping need no maths.
So dividing the laddoos uses maths.
Answer: Dividing 12 laddoos equally among 4 friends
quiz.mistake: Thinks maths is only done in a classroom

quiz.q: An election officer adds up the votes of every booth to find the winner. Which area of life is maths helping here?
quiz.explain: Counting and comparing votes is how a democracy decides who wins.
steps: The officer counts and adds votes from every booth.
Comparing the totals decides who wins the election.
Elections are how a democracy chooses its leaders.
quiz.mistake: Does not see vote-counting as mathematics

quiz.q: An engineer calculates how much weight a bridge can carry. Maths is helping in…
quiz.explain: Safe buildings and bridges need careful calculation of lengths, loads and angles.
steps: The engineer works out the load a bridge can safely carry.
This needs careful calculation of lengths, loads and angles.
That is part of building and construction.
So maths is helping in building and construction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks engineers just guess

quiz.q: Kiran sees that the street lights switch on a little earlier every evening in winter. What is the BEST mathematical next step?
options: Check the times each day and then try to explain why it happens
quiz.explain: A mathematician checks the pattern carefully and then looks for the reason behind it.
steps: Kiran has noticed a pattern in the switch-on times.
A mathematician first checks the pattern carefully (note the times each day).
Then she tries to explain why it happens.
Ignoring it or calling it magic is not maths → 'Check the times each day and then try to explain why it happens'.
Answer: Check the times each day and then try to explain why it happens
quiz.mistake: Stops at noticing the pattern without checking or explaining it

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'My cousin says maths is just doing sums. Is that all it is?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Maths is hunting for patterns and finding out why they happen. It's everywhere!
teach.nudge: But what does a mathematician look for, and what do they ask about it?

revise.summary: Mathematics is the search for patterns, and for explanations of why those patterns happen. It is both an art and a science, and it helps in daily life and in big things like science, democracy and building bridges.
focus: Say what mathematics is: patterns and why they happen
Explain why maths is both an art and a science
Give examples of where maths helps: gravitation, genomes, vote counting, bridges, shopping
Know the steps: describe the pattern, check it with data, then find why
remember: Mathematics is the search for patterns, and for explanations of why those patterns happen
Art: beautiful patterns to create and enjoy; science: exact rules that help us understand the world
Patterns in planet motion led to the idea of gravitation
traps: Maths is not only memorising tables or calculating
'Art' here does not mean only drawing or painting
Don't stop at noticing a pattern: check it and explain why it happens

learn.hook: If you know the secret rule, you can predict a number nobody has written yet. That's maths magic!
points: A number sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule, like 2, 4, 6, 8, ...
To find the rule, look at how each number changes into the next: do we add, subtract, multiply or double?
Famous sequences: counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ...; odd numbers 1, 3, 5, ...; powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...
Virahānka numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... : each number is the sum of the two numbers before it.

example.q: Find the next two numbers: 3, 7, 11, 15, ...
steps: The gaps are 7 − 3 = 4, 11 − 7 = 4, 15 − 11 = 4, so the rule is 'add 4'.

learn.reallife: Seat numbers in a train coach, house numbers on one side of a street (1, 3, 5, ...) and saving money that doubles all follow number sequences.

games.title: Match each sequence to its rule

quiz.q: What comes next: 4, 9, 14, 19, ...?
quiz.explain: Each number is 5 more than the one before, so 19 + 5 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Adds the wrong gap (4 or 6) or adds 10 instead of 5

quiz.q: Riya saves ₹1 on day 1, ₹2 on day 2, ₹4 on day 3, doubling every day. How much does she save on day 6?
quiz.explain: Doubling each day gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Day 6 is ₹32.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 each day instead of doubling, or counts one day too many or too few

quiz.q: The Virahānka numbers go 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... What is the next number?
quiz.explain: Each Virahānka number is the sum of the two before it, so 8 + 13 = 21.
steps: The two numbers before are 8 and 13
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed gap of 5 or doubles 13 instead of adding the last two numbers

quiz.q: Which number is missing: 81, 27, ___, 3, 1?
quiz.explain: Each number is the one before divided by 3: 27 ÷ 3 = 9, and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 fits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rule is 'subtract' instead of 'divide by 3'

quiz.q: Add the first five odd numbers: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = ?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25. Adding the first five odd numbers always gives 5 × 5, a square number.
quiz.mistake: Makes an adding slip or multiplies 5 × 4 or 5 × 6

quiz.q: Meena writes 100, 92, 84, 76, ... What is the 6th number in her list?
quiz.explain: The rule is 'subtract 8'. The list goes 100, 92, 84, 76, 68, 60, so the 6th number is 60.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 5th number (68) or goes one step too far (52)

quiz.q: Which sequence follows the rule 'multiply by 2'?
quiz.explain: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24. The others add 2, add 3 or multiply by 3.
steps: Check each sequence by dividing each term by the one before.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 3, 6, 9, 12 doubles because 3 to 6 is a double, without checking the next step

quiz.q: Cubes go 1, 8, 27, 64, ... What is the next cube?
quiz.explain: The 5th cube is 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
quiz.mistake: Works out 5 × 5 (a square) instead of 5 × 5 × 5

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Someone gave me 5, 10, 15, 20... How do I find the next number?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Find the rule, then use it again. I can predict numbers now!
teach.nudge: But how do I know what to do to get from one number to the next?

revise.summary: A number sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule. To find the rule, see how each number changes into the next: add, subtract, multiply or double.
focus: Find the rule of a sequence and write the next terms
Know the famous sequences: counting numbers, odd numbers, powers of 2, Virahānka numbers, cubes
Find a term at a given position without stopping early or going too far
remember: Virahānka numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...: each number is the sum of the two before it
traps: Don't add a fixed gap when the rule is doubling
Check more than one step: 3, 6, 9, 12 does not double just because 3 to 6 is a double
A cube is 5 × 5 × 5, not 5 × 5 (that is a square)

learn.hook: Can a picture of dots tell you the next number before you calculate it? Let's see!
points: Number theory is the part of maths that studies patterns in whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
The simplest sequence is all 1's: 1, 1, 1, 1, ... The rule is 'always write 1'.
Drawing dots shows why a sequence grows. Triangular numbers make triangles of dots, square numbers make squares and cube numbers make cubes, which is how they got their names.
To get the next triangle picture, add a new row with one more dot. To get the next square, add a new row and a new column.
Powers of 2 can be pictured by doubling a group of dots each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... Powers of 3 by making 3 copies each time: 1, 3, 9, 27, ...

example.q: A dot triangle has rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 dots. How many dots does the NEXT triangle picture have?
steps: The next picture adds a new bottom row with 5 dots.

learn.reallife: Bowling pins stand in a triangle (1, 2, 3, 4 = 10 pins) and a chessboard is a square of 8 × 8 = 64 squares.

items.q: Dots in a triangle with rows 1 to 6
Cubes in a 3 by 3 by 3 block

quiz.q: What is the 50th term of the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, ...?
quiz.explain: Every term of this sequence is 1, so the 50th term is 1 too.
steps: The sequence is 1, 1, 1, 1, … — every term is 1.
The rule never changes, so the 50th term is also 1.
50 is the position, not the term.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the position number is the term

quiz.q: Number theory studies patterns in…
quiz.explain: Number theory is the study of patterns in the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
steps: Number theory is a branch of maths.
It studies patterns in the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Shapes belong to geometry; colours, maps and music notes are not its topic.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up number theory with other subjects

quiz.q: Why are 1, 4, 9, 16, ... called square numbers?
options: Their dots can be arranged in a square
quiz.explain: 1, 4, 9, 16 dots can be arranged as 1×1, 2×2, 3×3 and 4×4 squares.
steps: Each number of dots makes a perfect square.
They are not all even (1, 9 are odd) and do not all end in 6.
So they are square numbers because their dots form a square.
Answer: Their dots can be arranged in a square
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the name with the dot picture

quiz.q: A square of dots has 7 rows of 7. To draw the next square picture, how many dots must be added?
quiz.explain: The next square is 8 × 8 = 64. 64 − 49 = 15 new dots (a new row and a new column sharing one corner dot).
quiz.mistake: Adds only a row of 8, or forgets the shared corner dot

quiz.q: Cube numbers 1, 8, 27, ... are named after the shape made by stacking small cubes. How many small cubes are in the 4th cube picture?
quiz.explain: The 4th cube is 4 small cubes long, 4 wide and 4 high: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.
quiz.mistake: Works out 4 × 4 (a square) instead of 4 × 4 × 4

quiz.q: A dot triangle picture has 28 dots. How many dots are in its bottom row?
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 28, so the bottom row has 7 dots.
quiz.mistake: Halves 28 instead of finding the rows

quiz.q: Ananya pictures powers of 2 by doubling a pile of beads: 1, 2, 4, 8. How many beads are in the 7th pile?
quiz.explain: Doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. The 7th pile has 64 beads.
quiz.mistake: Counts one doubling too many or too few

quiz.q: For powers of 3, each picture is made of 3 copies of the one before. The 3rd picture has 9 dots. How many dots does the 5th have?
quiz.explain: 9 × 3 = 27 for the 4th picture and 27 × 3 = 81 for the 5th.
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 instead of multiplying by 3, or stops one step early

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'Why do people call 9 a square number? It doesn't look square!'
teach.praise: Tweet! 9 dots fit in 3 rows of 3, which makes a square. Pictures explain the names!
teach.nudge: How could you arrange 9 things to show it is square?

revise.summary: Number theory studies patterns in whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, .... Drawing dots shows why sequences grow: triangular numbers make triangles, square numbers make squares and cube numbers make cubes.
focus: Know why square, triangular and cube numbers have those names
Grow a dot picture: next triangle adds a row with one more dot; next square adds a row and a column
Picture powers of 2 by doubling and powers of 3 by making 3 copies
remember: Number theory: the part of maths that studies patterns in whole numbers
All 1's: 1, 1, 1, 1, ... (rule: always write 1)
traps: In 1, 1, 1, ... every term is 1; the position number is not the term
Going from a 7 × 7 square to 8 × 8 adds 15 dots, not just a row of 8 (don't forget the corner dot)
For powers of 3, multiply by 3; don't add 3

learn.hook: Honeybees love hexagons. Mathematicians love hexagonal numbers: 1, 7, 19, 37, ...
points: Hexagonal numbers count dots that form a hexagon with a centre dot: 1, 7, 19, 37, 61, ...
Each new hexagon adds a ring around the old one. The rings have 6, 12, 18, 24, ... dots (multiples of 6).
Six times a triangular number plus 1 gives a hexagonal number: 6 × 1 + 1 = 7, 6 × 3 + 1 = 19, 6 × 6 + 1 = 37.
Adding hexagonal numbers from the start gives cube numbers: 1 = 1, 1 + 7 = 8, 1 + 7 + 19 = 27, 1 + 7 + 19 + 37 = 64. A cube seen from a corner looks like a hexagon!

example.q: Find the 5th hexagonal number.

learn.reallife: Honeycombs, the hexagonal tiles on some floors and a plate of 7 round puris (one in the middle, six around) show hexagon patterns.

quiz.q: What comes next: 1, 7, 19, 37, ...?
quiz.explain: The gaps are 6, 12, 18, so the next gap is 24: 37 + 24 = 61.
quiz.mistake: Uses the same gap of 18 again

quiz.q: How many dots are in the outer ring of the 4th hexagon picture (37 dots)?
quiz.explain: The 3rd hexagon has 19 dots, so the 4th ring adds 37 − 19 = 18 dots.
steps: The 4th picture has 37 dots and the 3rd has 19 dots.
So the outer ring has 18 dots.
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 × 4 instead of 6 × 3

quiz.q: Using '6 times a triangular number plus 1', which hexagonal number comes from the triangular number 15?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 1

quiz.explain: 1 + 7 + 19 = 27, which is the cube 3 × 3 × 3.
quiz.mistake: Makes an addition slip

quiz.q: Adding the first four hexagonal numbers gives which cube?
quiz.mistake: Adds only three of them, or picks the next cube

quiz.q: The first five hexagonal numbers add up to 125. What is 5 × 5 × 5?
quiz.explain: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125, so the sum of hexagonal numbers is again a cube.
steps: So 5 × 5 × 5 = 125, the same as the sum of the first five hexagonal numbers.
quiz.mistake: Works out 5 × 5 only

quiz.q: A plate holds 1 puri in the centre with 6 around it. A caterer adds the next full ring around it. How many puris are on the plate now?
quiz.explain: The second ring adds 12, so 7 + 12 = 19 puris, the 3rd hexagonal number.
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 again instead of 12

quiz.q: Which number is NOT a hexagonal number?
quiz.explain: Hexagonal numbers are 1, 7, 19, 37, 61... 27 is a cube number, not hexagonal.
steps: 27 is not in the list; it is 3 × 3 × 3, a cube number.
So 27 is NOT a hexagonal number.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up cube numbers with hexagonal numbers

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'How do I get the next hexagonal number after 19?'
teach.praise: Wow! Add a ring of 18 dots and 19 becomes 37. Hexagon power!
teach.nudge: How many dots go in the new ring around the hexagon?

revise.summary: Hexagonal numbers count dots that form a hexagon with a centre dot: 1, 7, 19, 37, 61, .... Each new hexagon adds a ring of 6, 12, 18, 24, ... dots, and adding hexagonal numbers from the start gives cube numbers.
focus: Continue the hexagonal numbers by adding rings of 6, 12, 18, ...
Use 'six times a triangular number plus 1'
Show that 1, 1 + 7, 1 + 7 + 19, ... give the cubes 1, 8, 27, ...
remember: Hexagonal numbers: 1, 7, 19, 37, 61, ...
Six times a triangular number plus 1 gives a hexagonal number: 6 × 3 + 1 = 19
traps: Don't use the same gap again: the rings grow by 6 each time (6, 12, 18, 24)
Don't forget to add 1 after multiplying by 6
Don't mix up cube numbers (like 27) with hexagonal numbers

learn.hook: Stack laddoos in a triangle or a square and you discover two of the most famous number families!
points: Triangular numbers count dots arranged in a triangle: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, ... The 5th one is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
Square numbers count dots arranged in a square: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... The 5th one is 5 × 5 = 25.
Adding odd numbers from 1 gives square numbers: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4 × 4.
Two triangular numbers next to each other add up to a square: 6 + 10 = 16.
Counting up and back down gives a square too: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9 = 3 × 3.

example.q: Find the 7th triangular number.

learn.reallife: Bowling pins and a carrom board's starting coins sit in triangles; chessboards and tiled floors show square numbers.

quiz.q: What is the 6th triangular number?
quiz.mistake: Gives the 5th triangular number (15) or the 6th square number (36)

quiz.q: What is the 8th square number?
quiz.explain: The 8th square number is 8 × 8 = 64.
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 + 8 = 16 instead of multiplying 8 × 8

quiz.q: Aisha arranges laddoos in a square tray with 9 rows and 9 laddoos in each row. How many laddoos are there?
quiz.explain: 9 rows of 9 is 9 × 9 = 81 laddoos, a square number.
quiz.mistake: Adds 9 + 9 instead of multiplying, or makes a times-table slip (72, 90)

quiz.explain: These are the first 6 odd numbers, and their sum is 6 × 6 = 36.
steps: Count the odd numbers: 6 of them
quiz.mistake: Forgets the last number (25) or makes an adding slip

quiz.q: Which two neighbouring triangular numbers add up to 25?
quiz.explain: 10 and 15 are next to each other in 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, and 10 + 15 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Picks 9 and 16, which add to 25 but are square numbers, not triangular ones

quiz.q: Harpreet stacks cricket balls in a triangle: 1 ball in the top row, 2 in the next, then 3, with 5 rows in all. How many balls does he use?
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, the 5th triangular number.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 4 rows (10) or uses the square number 5 × 5 = 25

quiz.explain: Counting up to 5 and back down to 1 gives 5 × 5 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Counts the 5 twice (30) or only adds one side (15)

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is BOTH a triangular number and a square number?
quiz.explain: 36 = 6 × 6 is square, and 36 = 1 + 2 + ... + 8 is the 8th triangular number. 16 and 25 are only square; 10 is only triangular.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one of the two lists

teach.ask: Gappu has a pile of laddoos: 'What is the difference between a triangular number and a square number?'
teach.praise: Wow! Triangles grow by adding 1, 2, 3, ... and squares are a number times itself. I'll stack my laddoos both ways!
teach.nudge: How do I actually work out a triangular number? And a square one?

revise.summary: Triangular numbers (1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ...) count dots in a triangle and square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...) count dots in a square. They are linked: adding odd numbers or two neighbouring triangular numbers gives a square.
focus: Find the nth triangular number (1 + 2 + ... + n) and the nth square number (n × n)
Use the links: odd numbers add to squares; two neighbouring triangular numbers add to a square
Use counting up and back down: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9
remember: 5th triangular number: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15
5th square number: 5 × 5 = 25
traps: A square number is 8 × 8, not 8 + 8
Don't mix up the 6th triangular number (21) with the 6th square number (36)
9 and 16 add to 25 but they are square numbers; the triangular pair is 10 and 15

learn.hook: Want to add the first 100 odd numbers in 2 seconds? A picture shows the trick.
points: Take a square of dots and split it into L-shapes from one corner. The L-shapes have 1, 3, 5, 7, ... dots.
So 1 + 3 + 5 + ... (the first n odd numbers) = n × n. The picture explains WHY it always works.
First 10 odd numbers: 1 + 3 + ... + 19 = 10 × 10 = 100. First 100 odd numbers: 100 × 100 = 10000.
The nth odd number is 2 × n − 1: the 10th is 19 and the 100th is 199.
A picture explanation works for every case, not only the few we checked. That is the power of an explanation.

steps: So we are adding the first 15 odd numbers.

learn.reallife: If you tile a square floor by adding L-shaped borders of tiles, the number of tiles in the borders goes 1, 3, 5, 7, ...

games.title: Picture proof check
items: An L-shape around a 3×3 square of dots has 7 dots.
The sum of the first 100 odd numbers is 10000.
Checking 3 examples proves a rule for all numbers.
A few examples are not enough; we need an explanation, like a picture.
The L-shapes in a square of dots go 1, 3, 5, 7, ...
Each L adds 2 more dots than the one before.

quiz.q: Find the sum of the first 10 odd numbers.
quiz.explain: The first 10 odd numbers add to 10 × 10 = 100.
steps: Sum of first n odd numbers = n × n
quiz.mistake: Adds the first 10 counting numbers (55) instead

quiz.q: Find the sum of the first 100 odd numbers.
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 × 10 or the sum of counting numbers

quiz.q: In a 6 × 6 square of dots split into L-shapes, how many dots are in the biggest (outer) L?
quiz.explain: The outer L has 6 × 6 − 5 × 5 = 36 − 25 = 11 dots, the 6th odd number.
steps: Inside it is a 5 × 5 square with 5 × 5 = 25 dots.
11 is the 6th odd number, so the answer is 11.
quiz.mistake: Counts the corner dot twice (12)

quiz.explain: 39 is the 20th odd number (2 × 20 − 1). So the sum is 20 × 20 = 400.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 39 is the 39th odd number or uses 19 × 19

quiz.q: What is the 25th odd number?
quiz.explain: The nth odd number is 2n − 1: 2 × 25 − 1 = 49.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2n or 2n + 1

quiz.q: The sum of some odd numbers starting from 1 is 81. How many odd numbers were added?
quiz.explain: 81 = 9 × 9, so 9 odd numbers were added (1 + 3 + ... + 17).
steps: Rule: 1 + 3 + 5 + … (first n odd numbers) = n × n.
Check: the 9th odd number is 2 × 9 − 1 = 17, and 1 + 3 + … + 17 = 81.
quiz.mistake: Gives the last odd number (17) instead of how many

quiz.q: Ravi adds 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 and gets 48. What should he get?
quiz.explain: These are the first 7 odd numbers, so the sum is 7 × 7 = 49.
steps: Rule: sum of first n odd numbers = n × n.
quiz.mistake: Makes an adding slip

quiz.q: Why does the dot picture prove that odd numbers add to squares?
options: Because it works for 1 and 3 only
Because any square of dots can be split into L-shapes of 1, 3, 5, ... dots
quiz.explain: Every square, however big, splits into L-shapes of consecutive odd numbers, so the rule always holds.
steps: Any n × n square of dots can be cut into L-shapes.
The L-shapes have 1, 3, 5, 7, … dots — the odd numbers in order.
This works for every square, however big, not just small ones.
So the picture proves that odd numbers add up to squares.
Answer: Because any square of dots can be split into L-shapes of 1, 3, 5, ... dots
quiz.mistake: Thinks a few examples are a proof

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Is there a shortcut to add 1 + 3 + 5 + ... all the way to the 50th odd number?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! 50 odd numbers make a 50 by 50 square: 2500!
teach.nudge: What shape do the odd numbers build together?

revise.summary: A square of dots splits into L-shapes of 1, 3, 5, 7, ... dots, so the first n odd numbers add up to n × n. The picture explains why it works for every case.
focus: Find the sum of the first n odd numbers as n × n
Find the nth odd number as 2 × n − 1
Work backwards: from a sum like 81, find how many odd numbers were added
Explain why a picture proves it but a few examples do not
remember: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... (first n odd numbers) = n × n
The nth odd number is 2 × n − 1: the 10th is 19, the 100th is 199
First 10 odd numbers: 1 + 3 + ... + 19 = 100
traps: Don't use 2n or 2n + 1 for the nth odd number
39 is the 20th odd number, not the 39th, so 1 + 3 + ... + 39 = 400

learn.hook: Every drawing in geometry is built from tiny dots and straight paths. Let's meet the building blocks!

quiz.q: Manu walks from his house to the shop. Which route is the shortest?
options: A curved path around the park
The straight path joining the two places
quiz.explain: The line segment joining two points is the shortest path between them.
steps: The shortest path between two points is the line segment joining them.
Zig-zag and curved paths are longer.
So the paths are not all the same.
The straight path is the shortest.
Answer: The straight path joining the two places
quiz.mistake: Thinks all routes are equally long

quiz.q: Four points A, B, C, D lie on one line in that order. How many line segments can be named using these points?
quiz.explain: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD: 6 segments.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the small pieces AB, BC, CD

quiz.q: A figure has one endpoint O and passes through T with an arrowhead after T. What is it?
quiz.explain: It starts at O and goes on through T, so it is ray OT.
steps: The figure has one endpoint O.
It goes through T and keeps going (arrowhead after T).
One endpoint and endless in one direction = a ray, named starting point first.
quiz.mistake: Writes the starting point last

quiz.q: Riya reads: 'Draw line l and mark a point A that is NOT on it.' Which drawing is right?
options: A dot A sitting on line l
A dot A away from line l
quiz.explain: Point A must be outside the line, so the dot is away from line l.
steps: The instruction says A is NOT on line l.
So the dot A must be drawn away from the line.
A dot on the line, crossing lines or a ray do not follow the instruction.
So the right drawing has dot A away from line l.
Answer: A dot A away from line l
quiz.mistake: Misses the word NOT

quiz.q: How many lines pass through the two points X and Y, and how many through X alone?
options: One through X and Y; endlessly many through X alone
quiz.explain: Exactly one line passes through two points, but endlessly many can pass through one point.
steps: Through two points X and Y: exactly one line.
Through one point X: we can turn the line in any direction, so endlessly many lines.
So: one through X and Y; endlessly many through X alone.
Answer: One through X and Y; endlessly many through X alone
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two cases

quiz.q: A line segment AB is 7 cm long. Point C is on AB so that AC = 3 cm. What is CB?
quiz.explain: CB = AB − AC = 7 − 3 = 4 cm.
steps: C lies on AB, so AC + CB = AB.
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I drew a long line on the wall. Did I draw the whole line?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A line never ends, so we draw only part of it with arrowheads.
teach.nudge: Does a line ever stop?

revise.summary: A line can be named by any two points on it or by one small letter, and it is drawn with arrowheads at both ends because it never ends. The straight path (a line segment) is the shortest route between two points.
focus: Name one line in different ways using points on it
Read figures: two endpoints = segment, one arrowhead = ray, arrowheads at both ends = line
Draw rough figures from statements, reading words like NOT carefully
Find a missing part of a segment by subtracting
remember: Line m = line AB = line AC when A, B, C lie on line m
Through two points: exactly one line; through one point: endlessly many lines
The straight path between two points is the shortest route
traps: A drawn line is only a part of the whole line
With 4 points on a line there are 6 segments, not just the 3 small pieces
If AB = 7 cm and AC = 3 cm, CB = 4 cm: subtract, don't add

learn.hook: Scissors, a compass and a half-open door all hide an angle. Can you name them?
points: An angle has a vertex (the common starting point) and two arms (the two rays).
We name an angle with three letters, the vertex in the middle: ∠ABC has vertex B and arms BA and BC. ∠CBA is the same angle.
If many angles share one vertex, the name ∠B is not clear. Use three letters to say exactly which angle you mean.
Angles are all around: open scissors, a compass, an opening door, a book, a clock's hands.
Rays from one point make many angles: 3 rays from O (OA, OB, OC) make ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠AOC.

example.q: Rays OP, OQ, OR, OS start from O, in that order. Name all the angles.

learn.reallife: A ceiling fan's blades meet at the centre making angles, and the hands of a clock form an angle at the centre.

items.text: The two rays of an angle are its ___
3 rays from one point make ___ angles

quiz.q: In ∠PQR, which point is the vertex?
quiz.explain: The middle letter is the vertex, so it is Q.
steps: Rule: in a three-letter angle name, the middle letter is the vertex.
In ∠PQR the middle letter is Q.
P and R are points on the arms.
quiz.mistake: Takes the first letter as the vertex

quiz.q: Which name is the same as ∠XYZ?
quiz.explain: Reversing the outer letters keeps Y in the middle: ∠ZYX.
steps: The vertex of ∠XYZ is Y, the middle letter.
Reversing the outer letters keeps Y in the middle: ∠ZYX.
∠YXZ, ∠XZY, ∠YZX have a different middle letter, so a different vertex.
quiz.mistake: Moves the vertex out of the middle

quiz.q: Three rays OA, OB, OC start at O. Why is '∠O' not a good name?
options: Because O is not a point
Because there are three angles at O, so ∠O does not say which one
quiz.explain: ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠AOC all have vertex O, so we need three letters.
steps: With rays OA, OB, OC there are three angles at O: ∠AOB, ∠BOC, ∠AOC.
'∠O' does not tell which of these we mean.
So we must use three letters.
Answer: Because there are three angles at O, so ∠O does not say which one
quiz.mistake: Thinks one letter is always enough

quiz.q: What are the arms of ∠MNP?
quiz.explain: The arms start at the vertex N and go through M and P.
steps: In ∠MNP the vertex is N (middle letter).
The arms start at N and pass through M and through P.
So the arms are NM and NP.
Arms always start at the vertex.
quiz.mistake: Starts the arms at the wrong point

quiz.q: Rays OA, OB, OC, OD start at O. How many angles are formed (smaller than a straight angle, with arms on these rays)?
quiz.explain: ∠AOB, ∠AOC, ∠AOD, ∠BOC, ∠BOD, ∠COD: 6 angles.
steps: Pair each ray with every ray after it.
OA with OB, OC, OD → 3; OB with OC, OD → 2; OC with OD → 1.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the angles between neighbouring rays

quiz.q: Five rays start from one point, all inside a quarter turn. How many angles do they make?
steps: Pair each ray with every ray after it.
quiz.mistake: Counts only neighbours (4) or one per ray (5)

quiz.q: When Asha opens a pair of scissors, where is the vertex of the angle?
options: At the tips of the blades
At the screw where the blades meet
quiz.explain: The blades turn about the screw, so that is the common point of the arms.
steps: The two blades are the arms of the angle.
They turn about the screw where they are joined.
The common point of the arms is the vertex.
So the vertex is at the screw.
Answer: At the screw where the blades meet
quiz.mistake: Picks the tips, where the arms end

quiz.q: Which everyday thing does NOT show an angle opening and closing?
options: A door turning on its hinges
A ball rolling on the ground
quiz.explain: A rolling ball has no two arms turning about a point.
steps: An angle needs two arms turning about a point.
A door (hinge), a book (spine) and compasses (top joint) all have this.
A rolling ball has no two arms turning about a point.
So the rolling ball does not show an angle.
Answer: A ball rolling on the ground
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything that moves makes an angle

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'Why can't I just call every angle at point B ∠B?'
teach.praise: Chirp! With many angles at B, three letters with B in the middle say exactly which one!
teach.nudge: What happens when two or three angles share the same vertex?

revise.summary: An angle has a vertex and two arms, and is named with three letters with the vertex in the middle. When many angles share a vertex, three letters say exactly which angle is meant.
focus: Find the vertex and arms from an angle's name
Explain why ∠B alone can be unclear
Count all the angles made by several rays from one point
Spot angles in daily life (scissors, doors, clock hands)
remember: ∠ABC has vertex B and arms BA and BC; ∠CBA is the same angle
3 rays from O make ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠AOC
4 rays from one point make 6 angles; 5 rays make 10
traps: The vertex is the middle letter, not the first
Don't count only the angles between neighbouring rays
The vertex of open scissors is at the screw, not at the tips

learn.hook: Which slice of pizza is bigger? Put one on top of the other and see!
points: To compare two angles, place one on top of the other with the vertices together and one arm on top of the other arm.
The angle whose second arm sticks out further is bigger. If the second arms also match, the angles are equal.
Equal angles have the same amount of turn, even if they look different because of their position.
If you cannot move the angles, put a transparent circle with its centre on each vertex and mark where the arms cross it. More of the circle between the arms means a bigger angle.
Folding a paper makes creases and angles. Name them, then compare them to find the largest and smallest.

example.q: ∠A is put on ∠B with vertices together and one arm matching. The other arm of ∠A lies inside ∠B. Which is bigger?
steps: ∠A's other arm is inside ∠B, so ∠A turns less.

learn.reallife: Tailors compare collar angles by laying one piece on another, and carpenters check corners by fitting a set-square.

games.title: Compare carefully
items: To compare angles, the vertices must be placed together.
Otherwise the turns cannot be matched.
An angle drawn with longer arms is always bigger.
Only the turn matters, not arm length.
If both arms match after superimposing, the angles are equal.
They have the same turn.
A transparent circle can compare angles that cannot be moved.
Compare how much of the circle lies between the arms.
An angle that looks tilted is smaller.
Turning an angle round does not change its size.

games.title: Smallest to biggest turn
items: A quarter of a right angle
Half a right angle
A right angle
Half a full turn
Three quarters of a full turn

quiz.q: Ravi superimposes ∠P on ∠Q with vertices and one arm matching. The other arm of ∠P is outside ∠Q. What can he say?
quiz.explain: ∠P turns further, so it is bigger.
steps: The vertices and one arm match.
The other arm of ∠P lies outside ∠Q.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'outside' means smaller

quiz.q: When comparing two angles by putting one on the other, what must match first?
quiz.explain: Put the vertices together and lay one arm along the other arm.
steps: To compare, put one angle on top of the other.
First the vertices must match, and one arm must lie along the other arm.
Then see where the second arms fall.
Arm lengths, colours or letters do not matter.
Answer: The vertices and one arm
quiz.mistake: Lines up the arm ends instead of the vertices

quiz.q: ∠X = 40° is drawn with 2 cm arms, ∠Y = 40° with 9 cm arms but turned sideways. Which is true?
quiz.explain: Both have the same turn of 40°, so they are equal.
steps: The size of an angle is the amount of turn, not the arm length or the way it faces.
quiz.mistake: Is fooled by arm length or position

quiz.q: Using a transparent circle centred at the vertex, ∠A covers 3 marks of the circle and ∠B covers 5 equal marks. Which is bigger?
quiz.explain: More of the circle between the arms means more turn, so ∠B is bigger.
steps: The circle is centred at the vertex and split into equal marks.
More marks between the arms = more turn.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fewer marks means bigger

quiz.q: Why do we centre the transparent circle on the vertex?
options: So the circle measures the turn about the vertex
Because arms must touch the edge
quiz.explain: The turn happens about the vertex, so the circle must be centred there.
steps: An angle is a turn about its vertex.
To measure that turn, the circle must be centred on the vertex.
Then the part of the circle between the arms shows the turn.
So we centre it to measure the turn about the vertex.
Answer: So the circle measures the turn about the vertex
quiz.mistake: Places the circle anywhere

quiz.q: A paper is folded once, then folded again so the first crease falls on itself. The two creases make four angles at the centre. What are they like?
quiz.explain: Folding the crease onto itself splits the straight angle into two equal halves, giving four right angles.
steps: The first fold makes a straight crease (a straight angle).
Folding the crease onto itself splits the straight angle into two equal halves.
Each half is a right angle, and the second crease makes four of them.
So all four are equal right angles.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that the folds make equal halves

quiz.q: A fan has three angles between its blades. Two are equal and the third is larger. If the equal ones are 100° each, how big is the third?
quiz.explain: The three angles make a full turn: 360 − 100 − 100 = 160°.
steps: The three angles around the centre make a full turn: 360°.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the angles make a full turn

quiz.q: Meera says ∠ABC is bigger than ∠DEF because ∠ABC's arms are longer. What is her mistake?
options: Arm length does not decide the size of an angle
quiz.explain: Size is the amount of turn between the arms, not the arm length.
steps: The size of an angle is the amount of turn between its arms.
Longer arms do not mean more turn.
So Meera cannot say ∠ABC is bigger just because its arms are longer.
Her mistake: arm length does not decide the size of an angle.
Answer: Arm length does not decide the size of an angle
quiz.mistake: Judges angles by arm length

teach.ask: Gappu has two paper angles. 'How do I find which one is bigger?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Vertex on vertex, arm on arm, then see which other arm turns further!
teach.nudge: Where should the two angles touch when you put them together?

revise.summary: To compare two angles, place one on the other with vertices together and one arm on one arm; the one whose second arm sticks out further is bigger. Arm length and position do not change the size of an angle.
focus: Compare angles by superimposing: match vertices and one arm first
Use a transparent circle centred on the vertex to compare turns
Recognise equal angles even when arm lengths or positions differ
remember: Bigger angle: its second arm sticks out further when vertices and one arm match
Equal angles have the same amount of turn
More of the circle between the arms means a bigger angle
traps: Arm length does not decide the size of an angle
Don't line up the arm ends; line up the vertices and one arm
Don't place the circle anywhere: centre it on the vertex

topics.title: Angles as turns: right and straight angles

learn.hook: Two straws and a paper clip can make every angle there is!
points: Join two straws with a clip so one can turn: this rotating-arms model shows an angle as a turn.
To copy an angle cut as a slit, open the arms until they pass exactly through the slit. That opening is the same angle.
A straight angle is a half turn. Half of a straight angle is a right angle, a quarter turn.
Fold a paper once to get a straight edge, then fold that edge onto itself: the corner you get is a right angle.
On dot grids you can join points to make straight angles (three dots in a line) and right angles (like the corner of a square).

example.q: Rays OA, OB, OC, OD fan out from O, all inside a right angle. How many acute angles are there?
steps: Every angle between these rays is less than 90°, so all are acute.

learn.reallife: Opening a laptop lid, turning a door key and opening a gate all turn an arm about a point, just like the straw model.

items.q: Degrees in half a straight angle
Right angles in a straight angle
Right angles in a full turn

Acute angles made by 5 rays inside a right angle

games.title: Turn true or false
items: A right angle is half of a straight angle.
Folding a paper twice correctly makes a right angle.
The second fold halves the straight crease.
Opening the straw model wider makes a smaller angle.
More turn means a bigger angle.
Three dots in a straight row make a straight angle at the middle dot.
The two arms point in opposite directions.
Making the straws longer changes the angle.
Angle size does not depend on arm length.

quiz.q: A right angle is what part of a straight angle?
quiz.explain: A straight angle is 180° and a right angle is 90°: one half.
steps: So a right angle is one half of a straight angle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a right angle is a quarter of a straight angle

quiz.q: How can you make a right angle with just a sheet of paper?
options: Fold it once, then fold the crease onto itself
quiz.explain: The first fold makes a straight edge; folding that onto itself halves it into right angles.
steps: Fold the paper once to get a straight edge (a straight angle).
This halves the straight angle, giving right angles.
So fold once, then fold the crease onto itself.
Answer: Fold it once, then fold the crease onto itself
quiz.mistake: Thinks one fold is enough

quiz.q: Sahil sets his straw model to pass through an angle-shaped slit cut in a card. What has he done?
options: Measured the length of the slit
Copied the angle of the slit
quiz.explain: When the arms just fit the slit, the model's opening equals the slit's angle.
steps: The straw model's arms are set to just fit the slit.
Then its opening matches the slit's opening.
So he has copied the angle of the slit.
He has not measured its length or made a straight angle.
Answer: Copied the angle of the slit
quiz.mistake: Thinks the model measures length

quiz.q: Six rays start from one point, all within a right angle. How many acute angles do they make?
quiz.explain: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 acute angles.
steps: Six rays within a right angle: every pair makes an acute angle.
1st ray pairs with 5, 2nd with 4, 3rd with 3, 4th with 2, 5th with 1.
quiz.mistake: Counts only neighbouring angles (5)

quiz.q: On a dot grid, which three dots make a straight angle at the middle dot B?
options: A, B, C in one straight row
A, B, C forming an L
A, B, C forming a triangle
quiz.explain: A straight angle needs the arms in opposite directions, so the dots must be in a line.
steps: A straight angle has its two arms pointing in opposite directions.
So A, B and C must lie in one straight line with B in the middle.
An L-shape gives a right angle; a triangle shape gives a smaller angle.
So A, B, C in one straight row.
Answer: A, B, C in one straight row
quiz.mistake: Thinks an L-shape is straight

quiz.q: A clock's minute hand moves from 12 to 6. Through what angle does it turn?
quiz.explain: 12 to 6 is a half turn: a straight angle of 180°.
steps: 12 to 6 is half way round the clock.
A full turn is 360°, so a half turn is 360 ÷ 2 = 180°.
quiz.mistake: Calls it a quarter turn

quiz.q: How many right angles make one full turn?
quiz.explain: 360 ÷ 90 = 4 right angles.
steps: A full turn = 360°; a right angle = 90°.
So 4 right angles make a full turn.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a full turn is two right angles

quiz.q: On a square dot grid, Neha joins one dot to the dot just to its right, and also to the dot just above it. What angle forms at the first dot?
quiz.explain: One arm goes along the row and the other up the column, which makes a right angle.
steps: One arm goes along the row (to the right).
The other goes up the column (straight up).
A row and a column meet like the corner of a square.
So the angle is a right angle.
quiz.mistake: Cannot see the square corner on a grid

teach.ask: Gappu has two straws and a clip. 'How can I show a right angle with them?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Open a quarter turn, which is half a straight angle. That's a right angle!
teach.nudge: How much should the straw turn compared to a straight angle?

revise.summary: An angle can be seen as a turn, like two joined straws turning. A straight angle is a half turn, and a right angle, half of a straight angle, is a quarter turn.
focus: Know a straight angle is a half turn and a right angle is a quarter turn
Make a right angle by folding paper twice
Find straight and right angles on dot grids and clocks
Count acute angles made by rays inside a right angle
remember: Straight angle = half turn; right angle = half of a straight angle = quarter turn
Fold paper once for a straight edge, then fold that edge onto itself for a right angle
4 right angles make one full turn
traps: A right angle is half of a straight angle, not a quarter of it
One fold is not enough to make a right angle
Six rays inside a right angle make 15 acute angles, not 5

learn.hook: How much does a door open? How far do clock hands turn? Degrees tell us exactly!
points: The size of an angle is the amount of turn between its arms. We measure it in degrees (°).
A full turn is 360°, a half turn (straight angle) is 180° and a quarter turn (right angle) is 90°.
Using a protractor: put its centre on the vertex, line up the baseline with one arm, and read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm.
Longer or shorter arms do not change the angle. Only the opening matters.
On a clock, the hour marks are 360° ÷ 12 = 30° apart.

example.q: What is the smaller angle between the clock hands at 4 o'clock?
steps: At 4:00 the hands are 4 gaps apart

learn.reallife: A cricket coach talks about the angle of the bat, and a fan blade or a door hinge turns through angles.

quiz.q: How many degrees are there in a quarter turn?
quiz.explain: A full turn is 360°, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.

quiz.q: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at 2:00?

learn.hook: Why not 100 degrees in a circle? Nobody knows for sure, but there are some clever ideas!
points: Nobody knows for sure why we use 360. One idea: many ancient calendars (in India, Persia, Babylonia and Egypt) used a year of 360 days. Another: the Babylonians counted in sixties (base 60), and 360 = 6 × 60.
360 has many divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, ... So a full turn splits into many equal whole-number angles.
Each equal part of a circle split into n parts is 360° ÷ n: 2 parts → 180°, 3 → 120°, 4 → 90°, 5 → 72°, 6 → 60°, 8 → 45°, 9 → 40°, 10 → 36°, 12 → 30°.
A paper protractor: fold a paper circle in half (180°), again (90°), again (45°) and once more (22½°). Mark the creases to measure angles roughly.

quiz.q: A cycle wheel has 36 equally spaced spokes. What is the angle between neighbouring spokes?

quiz.q: Why was 360 a good choice for a full turn?
options: It has very many divisors, so a turn splits into many equal whole parts
quiz.explain: 360 divides exactly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 and more.
steps: So a full turn can be split into many equal whole-number parts.
360 is not prime, not the biggest number and not a palindrome.
So it was a good choice because it has very many divisors.
Answer: It has very many divisors, so a turn splits into many equal whole parts
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number was chosen at random

quiz.q: Which of these is linked to the history of 360 degrees?
options: The number of bones in the body
The number of states in India
A year of about 360 days in ancient calendars
quiz.explain: One likely reason: many ancient calendars used a year of 360 days, and the Babylonians counted in sixties. Historians are not completely sure.
steps: Many ancient calendars used a year of about 360 days.
One full turn of the Sun's path could be split into one degree per day.
Bones, states and the speed of light are not linked to it.
So the answer is the 360-day year (historians are not completely sure).
Answer: A year of about 360 days in ancient calendars
quiz.mistake: Does not know the history

quiz.q: Which number does NOT divide 360 exactly?

quiz.mistake: Assumes 360 divides by everything up to 12

learn.hook: A protractor has two scales. Read the wrong one and 40° becomes 140°!
points: Always start from the 0 that lies on one arm. If you read the other scale, you get 180° minus the right answer.
Common mistakes: centre not on the vertex, base line not along an arm, or reading the wrong scale.
An angle bisector is a ray that splits an angle into two equal angles. Fold the paper so the two arms lie on each other: the crease is the bisector.
Measure the three angles of any triangle and add them: you always get about 180°. This guess (a conjecture) is true for every triangle.

example.q: A protractor shows 65 on the inner scale and 115 on the outer scale. The arm on the base line is at the inner scale's 0. What is the angle?
steps: Use the scale that starts at 0 on the arm: the inner scale.
The angle is 65°. (115° would be the wrong scale: 180 − 65.)

games.title: Spot the mistake

An acute angle is less than 90°.

The angles of a triangle add to about 180°.

quiz.q: Ayaan measures an obviously acute angle and writes 130°. What is the correct measure most likely to be?

steps: The angle is clearly acute (less than 90°), so 130° must be a misreading.
He read the other scale; the two scales add to 180°.
So the angle is most likely 50°.
quiz.mistake: Trusts a reading that does not match the angle type

quiz.q: Which mistake gives a wrong protractor reading?
options: Putting the centre on the vertex
Placing the centre away from the vertex
Putting the base line along one arm
Starting from the 0 on an arm
quiz.explain: The centre must be exactly on the vertex.
steps: Correct use: centre on the vertex, base line along one arm, start from 0 on that arm.
Placing the centre away from the vertex gives a wrong reading.
The other three options are correct steps.
So the mistake is placing the centre away from the vertex.
Answer: Placing the centre away from the vertex
quiz.mistake: Does not know the correct method

quiz.q: A ray bisects a 110° angle. What is each part?
steps: A bisector splits an angle into two equal parts.
quiz.mistake: Doubles instead of halving

quiz.q: How can you find the bisector of an angle drawn on paper without a protractor?
options: Fold so the two arms lie on each other; the crease is the bisector
quiz.explain: Folding one arm onto the other splits the turn into two equal parts.
steps: A bisector splits an angle into two equal parts.
Fold the paper so one arm lies exactly on the other arm.
The crease through the vertex divides the angle equally.
So the crease is the bisector.
Answer: Fold so the two arms lie on each other; the crease is the bisector
quiz.mistake: Folds anywhere

quiz.q: Tara measures a triangle's angles as 50° and 75°. What should the third angle be?
quiz.explain: The angles add to 180°: 180 − 50 − 75 = 55°.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two angles and stops

quiz.q: A bisector splits ∠AOB into two angles of 35° each. What is ∠AOB?
quiz.explain: Both halves together: 35 + 35 = 70°.
steps: The bisector makes two equal parts of 35° each.
quiz.mistake: Gives the half instead of the whole

quiz.q: Ishita measured a triangle's angles as 60°, 60° and 80°. What can we say?
options: There is a measuring mistake, because they add to 200°, not 180°
quiz.explain: The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so 200° means a mistake.
steps: The angles of a triangle always add up to 180°.
200° ≠ 180°, so at least one angle was measured wrongly.
So there is a measuring mistake.
Answer: There is a measuring mistake, because they add to 200°, not 180°
quiz.mistake: Does not check the angle sum

quiz.q: Arm OA lies on the base line where the OUTER scale reads 0. Arm OB crosses 30 on the inner scale and 150 on the outer scale. What is ∠AOB?
quiz.explain: Read the scale whose 0 is on arm OA: the outer scale. It shows 150°.
steps: Arm OA lies on the 0 of the OUTER scale.
So read the outer scale where arm OB crosses.
quiz.mistake: Reads the scale that does not start at 0 on an arm

teach.ask: Gappu has a paper angle of 80°. 'How do I cut it into two equal angles?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Fold arm onto arm, and the crease is the bisector: two 40° angles!
teach.nudge: How would you make the two arms meet?

revise.summary: Common protractor mistakes are a centre off the vertex, a base line not along an arm, or reading the wrong scale. An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal angles, and a triangle's three angles always add up to 180°.
focus: Spot and fix protractor mistakes; check the reading matches the angle type
Find the bisector by folding the arms onto each other
Use the triangle angle sum of 180° to find or check angles
remember: Reading the other scale gives 180° minus the right answer
Angle bisector: a ray that splits an angle into two equal angles
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°
traps: Don't trust a reading that does not match the angle type (an acute angle is not 130°)
Don't double when bisecting: halve (110° → 55°)
Read the scale that starts at 0 on an arm

learn.hook: Can you guess an angle just by looking? Play the estimation game and find out!
points: To draw ∠ABC = 70°: draw arm BC with a ruler. Put the protractor centre on B and the base line along BC.
Find 70 on the scale that starts at 0 on BC, mark a dot A there, remove the protractor and join BA.
For an angle more than 180°, like 250°, draw 360° − 250° = 110° and mark the outside (reflex) part.
To copy an angle, measure it first, then draw a new angle of the same measure.
Estimation game: guess an angle, then measure. The closer your guess, the higher your score. Comparing with 90° and 45° helps you guess.

example.q: Draw ∠PQR = 110°.
steps: Draw QR = 6 cm with a ruler.
Put the protractor's centre on Q and its base line on QR.
Using the scale that starts at 0 on QR, mark P at 110.

quiz.q: To draw ∠XYZ = 40°, where should the protractor's centre be?
quiz.explain: Y is the vertex (middle letter), so the centre goes on Y.
steps: In ∠XYZ the middle letter Y is the vertex.
The protractor's centre must sit on the vertex.
So place the centre on Y.
X and Z are on the arms.
quiz.mistake: Puts the centre on an arm's end

quiz.q: Kriti wants to draw a 75° angle, but she marks her dot at 75 on the WRONG scale (the one that does not start at 0 on her arm). What angle does she actually draw?
quiz.explain: On the correct scale that point reads 180 − 75 = 105°, so she draws 105°.
steps: She used the scale that does not start at 0 on her arm.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the wrong scale

quiz.q: To draw a reflex angle of 300°, which angle can you draw first?
quiz.explain: 360 − 300 = 60°. Draw 60°, then the reflex angle is the outside part.
steps: A protractor reads only up to 180°.
A reflex angle of 300° leaves 360 − 300 = 60° on the other side.
Draw 60°; the outside part is the 300° reflex angle.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 180 instead of 360

quiz.q: In the estimation game Manav guesses 50° and the angle measures 62°. By how many degrees was he off?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of finding the difference

quiz.q: Which angle is a good first guess for an angle that is just a bit wider than the corner of a page?
quiz.explain: A page corner is 90°, so a bit wider is about 95°.
steps: The corner of a page is a right angle, 90°.
'A bit wider' means a little more than 90°.
95° fits; 45° and 20° are smaller, 170° is much wider.
So a good first guess is 95°.
quiz.mistake: Does not use 90° as a benchmark

quiz.q: To copy ∠ABC onto another page, what should you do first?
options: Measure the lengths of the arms only
quiz.explain: Measure the angle, then draw a new angle with the same measure.
steps: To copy an angle, we need its size.
Then draw a new angle with the same measure.
Arm lengths do not decide the angle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks arm length must be copied

quiz.q: Ritu draws ∠PQR = 110°. Which type of angle is it?
quiz.explain: 110° is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.
steps: Acute < 90°; right = 90°; obtuse between 90° and 180°; reflex between 180° and 360°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up obtuse and reflex

quiz.q: To draw 135°, a quick way is to draw a straight angle and then…
quiz.explain: 180 − 45 = 135, so draw the straight angle and mark 45° back from one side.
steps: So draw the straight angle and mark 45° back from one side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 135° is more than 180°

teach.ask: Gappu has a protractor and ruler. 'How do I draw an angle of 60°?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Arm, centre on the vertex, start at 0, mark 60, join. Perfect!
teach.nudge: Where do you put the centre of the protractor?

revise.summary: To draw an angle, draw one arm, put the protractor centre on its endpoint and the base line along it, mark the angle on the scale that starts at 0 on that arm, and join. For an angle more than 180°, draw 360° minus it and mark the reflex part.
focus: Draw an angle of a given size with the protractor centred on the vertex
Draw a reflex angle using 360° minus it
Copy an angle by measuring it first
Estimate angles using 90° and 45° as benchmarks
remember: To draw ∠ABC = 70°: draw BC, centre on B, base line on BC, mark 70 on the scale from 0 on BC, join BA
Reflex angle 250°: draw 360° − 250° = 110° and mark the outside part
traps: Don't mark the dot on the wrong scale: 75° would become 105°
For a reflex angle, subtract from 360, not 180
Don't mix up obtuse (between 90° and 180°) and reflex (more than 180°)

learn.hook: Angles have names, just like cricket shots! Sharp, square, wide and more.
points: An acute angle is more than 0° but less than 90°, like the tip of a pizza slice.
A right angle is exactly 90°, like the corner of a book. It is marked with a small square.
An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°.
A straight angle is exactly 180°. A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°.
Two lines that meet at a right angle are called perpendicular lines.

example.q: What type of angle is 135°?

learn.reallife: The corner of a door is a right angle, an open laptop screen usually makes an obtuse angle, and scissors open a little make an acute angle.

games.title: Angle facts
items: An angle of 90° is an acute angle.
90° is exactly a right angle. Acute angles are less than 90°.
Every obtuse angle is bigger than every acute angle.
Obtuse angles are more than 90° and acute angles are less than 90°.
A straight angle measures 180°.
A straight angle is a half turn.
Two acute angles always add up to an obtuse angle.
20° + 30° = 50°, which is still acute.
The clock hands at 3:00 make a right angle.
3 hour-gaps × 30° = 90°.
A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°.
That is the meaning of reflex.

quiz.q: What type of angle is 72°?
quiz.explain: 72° is less than 90°, so it is acute.
steps: It is not obtuse, right or reflex.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the meanings of acute and obtuse

quiz.q: What type of angle is 145°?
quiz.explain: 145° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
steps: Obtuse angles are more than 90° and less than 180°.
It is not acute, straight or reflex.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any angle over 90° is reflex

quiz.q: The hands of a clock at 3:00 make which type of angle?
quiz.explain: At 3:00 the hands are 3 × 30° = 90° apart, which is a right angle.
steps: Each hour gap on a clock = 360 ÷ 12 = 30°.
At 3:00 the hands are 3 gaps apart: 3 × 30° = 90°.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the picture without working out the degrees

quiz.q: Aisha opens a book flat on the table so its two covers lie in one straight line. What angle do the covers make?
quiz.explain: Covers lying in one straight line make a straight angle of 180°.
steps: The two covers lie in one straight line.
Arms in opposite directions make a straight angle.
So the covers make a straight angle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a flat, open book makes a right angle

quiz.q: Which of these is a reflex angle?
quiz.explain: A reflex angle is between 180° and 360°. Only 250° fits.
steps: A reflex angle is between 180° and 360°.
quiz.mistake: Picks 170°, which is obtuse because it is less than 180°

quiz.q: Two lines cross so that all four angles are right angles. What are these lines called?
quiz.explain: Lines that meet at right angles are perpendicular. Parallel lines never meet at all.
steps: The lines meet so that all four angles are right angles.
Lines meeting at right angles are perpendicular.
Parallel lines never meet at all.
quiz.mistake: Confuses perpendicular with parallel

quiz.q: Joseph says the smaller angle between the clock hands at 10:00 is obtuse. Is he right?
options: No, it is a right angle
No, it is 60°, an acute angle
quiz.explain: From 10 to 12 is 2 hour-gaps: 2 × 30° = 60°, which is acute.
steps: Answer: No, it is 60°, an acute angle
quiz.mistake: Counts the gaps the long way round or miscounts

quiz.q: An angle is split into two equal parts of 50° each. What type is the whole angle?
quiz.explain: The whole angle is 50° + 50° = 100°, which is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Looks at one part (50°, acute) instead of the whole angle

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'Acute, right, obtuse, straight... how do I tell which is which?'
teach.praise: Yay! Less than 90° is acute, exactly 90° is right, between 90° and 180° is obtuse, 180° is straight. I'm an angle expert!

revise.summary: Angles are named by size: acute (less than 90°), right (exactly 90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (exactly 180°) and reflex (between 180° and 360°). Lines meeting at a right angle are perpendicular.

Find clock-hand angles and then name their type
Know that perpendicular lines meet at a right angle
remember: Acute: more than 0° but less than 90°; right: exactly 90°
Obtuse: more than 90° but less than 180°; straight: exactly 180°
Reflex: more than 180° but less than 360°
traps: Not every angle over 90° is reflex: 170° is obtuse
A flat, open book makes a straight angle, not a right angle
Don't confuse perpendicular with parallel

learn.hook: The Ashoka Chakra on our flag hides a neat angle puzzle!
points: Two angles that sit side by side on a straight line add up to 180°. If one is 130°, the other is 50°.
Letters can be drawn using given angles: the letter M has two slanting middle strokes; the letter Y has a stem and two arms making angles at the joint.
The angles around a point add to 360°. Around the joint of the letter Y, the three angles make a full turn.
The Ashoka Chakra has 24 equally spaced spokes, so the angle between neighbouring spokes is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°.

quiz.q: A see-saw plank makes an angle of 35° with the ground on one side. What angle does it make on the other side (along the ground line)?

Count gaps, not spokes, when finding angles on the Ashoka Chakra

Angles around a point add up to 360°
Ashoka Chakra: 360° ÷ 24 = 15°

learn.hook: Five friends stand in a line and each shouts one number. From just those numbers, can you work out who is tallest?
points: We use numbers to count (5 mangoes), measure (3 kg), label (bus number 42) and compare (Riya is 2 cm taller).
Game: children stand in a row (all of different heights). Each child says how many of their neighbours are taller: 0, 1 or 2.
A child at either end has only one neighbour, so they can only say 0 or 1. Only a middle child can say 2.
The tallest child always says 0, because nobody is taller than them.
Some lists of numbers are impossible. In a row of 3, '1, 1, 1' cannot happen: if both end children say 1, the middle child is tallest and must say 0.

example.q: Three children stand in a row and say 0, 2, 0. Is this possible? If so, who is shortest?
steps: The middle child says 2, so both neighbours are taller than the middle child.
The end children say 0, so nobody next to them is taller. That fits.
So it is possible, and the middle child is the shortest.
example.answer: Possible; the middle child is shortest

'Platform number 4' gives the platform a name.
It does not count how many platforms there are.
So the number is used to label.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a number to measure?
quiz.explain: 6 m is a length, so it measures.
steps: Measuring tells how long, heavy or big something is, with a unit.
'The rope is 6 m long' gives a length in metres.
Room 12 and Bus 501 are labels; 3 pencils is a count.
So 'The rope is 6 m long' measures.
Answer: The rope is 6 m long
quiz.mistake: Mixes up labels and measures

quiz.q: Four children in a row say 0, 1, ?, 0. What must the third child say?
quiz.explain: Child 4 says 0, so child 4 is taller than child 3. Child 1 says 0, so child 1 is taller than child 2; child 2 says 1, so child 3 is shorter than child 2. Both neighbours of child 3 are taller: it says 2.
steps: Child 2 already has one taller neighbour (child 1), so child 3 is shorter than child 2
quiz.mistake: Forgets to check both neighbours

quiz.q: In the taller-neighbour game, which child must say 0?
quiz.explain: No one is taller than the tallest child.
steps: Each child says how many neighbours are taller than them.
No one is taller than the tallest child.
So the tallest child has 0 taller neighbours.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up tallest and shortest

quiz.q: Can a child at the end of the row say 2?
options: No, an end child has only one neighbour
quiz.explain: An end child has one neighbour, so at most 1.
steps: A child at the end of the row has only one neighbour.
So at most 1 neighbour can be taller.
So no, an end child cannot say 2.
Answer: No, an end child has only one neighbour
quiz.mistake: Forgets that ends have one neighbour

quiz.q: Five children in a row say 1, 0, 2, 0, 1. Which children are taller than both their neighbours?
quiz.explain: Children saying 0 have no taller neighbour, so the 2nd and 4th are the 'peaks'.
steps: A child who says 0 has no taller neighbour.
So that child is taller than both (or all) of their neighbours.
In 1, 0, 2, 0, 1 the zeros are said by the 2nd and 4th children.
So the 2nd and 4th are taller than both their neighbours.
quiz.mistake: Thinks saying 1 means being tall

quiz.q: Three children say 1, 1, 1. Why is this impossible?
options: If both ends say 1, the middle child is taller than both and must say 0
Because three children cannot stand in a row
quiz.explain: Both end children have only the middle child as a neighbour, so the middle one is taller than both and says 0.
steps: Each end child has only one neighbour: the middle child.
If both ends say 1, the middle child is taller than both of them.
Then nobody is taller than the middle child, so it must say 0, not 1.
Answer: If both ends say 1, the middle child is taller than both and must say 0
quiz.mistake: Does not reason about who is taller than whom

quiz.q: A row of 4 children says 0, 1, 2, 0. Is this possible?
options: No, a child can never say 2
No, the 3rd child would have to be the tallest
No, two children cannot both say 0
quiz.explain: Heights 4, 3, 1, 2 (in that order) work: the answers are 0, 1, 2, 0.

learn.hook: Be the boss of your neighbours! A supercell beats everyone next to it.
points: In a table of numbers, a cell's neighbours are the cells just left, right, above and below it (not the diagonal ones).
A supercell is a cell whose number is greater than all of its neighbours.
The largest number in the table is always a supercell. The smallest number can never be a supercell.
Two neighbouring cells can never both be supercells, because one of them is smaller than the other.
To get the most supercells, put big numbers in cells that do not touch, like the black squares of a chessboard.

example.q: In the table 3 8 2 / 9 1 7 / 4 6 5, which cells are supercells?
steps: 6: neighbours 1, 4, 5 → supercell. 5: neighbours 7 and 6 are bigger → not.

learn.reallife: Like the tallest tree in a garden that stands above every tree around it, a supercell stands above its neighbours.

games.title: Supercell facts
items: The biggest number in a table is always a supercell.
Nothing near it is bigger.
The smallest number can be a supercell.
Each of its neighbours is bigger.
Two cells side by side can both be supercells.
One of them is smaller than the other.
Diagonal cells count as neighbours.
Only left, right, above and below count.
In a row of 5 cells, at most 3 can be supercells.

quiz.q: In the row 12, 30, 25, 41, 18, how many supercells are there?
quiz.explain: 30 beats 12 and 25; 41 beats 25 and 18. 12, 25 and 18 each have a bigger neighbour. So 2.
quiz.mistake: Counts the end numbers as supercells without checking

quiz.q: Why can the smallest number in a table never be a supercell?
options: Because all its neighbours are bigger
Because it is in a corner
quiz.explain: Every other number is bigger, so its neighbours are bigger.
steps: A supercell must be bigger than all its neighbours.
The smallest number in the table is smaller than every other number.
So all its neighbours are bigger than it.
It can never be a supercell.
Answer: Because all its neighbours are bigger
quiz.mistake: Thinks position decides it

quiz.q: In the table 7 2 / 3 9, which numbers are supercells?
quiz.explain: 7: neighbours 2 and 3 → supercell. 9: neighbours 2 and 3 → supercell.
steps: 2 and 3 have bigger neighbours, so the supercells are 7 and 9.
quiz.mistake: Counts diagonal cells as neighbours

quiz.q: What is the greatest number of supercells possible in a row of 7 cells?
quiz.explain: Supercells cannot sit side by side, so use cells 1, 3, 5, 7: 4 supercells.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every other cell starting from cell 2

quiz.q: A 3 by 3 table holds 1 to 9. To get 5 supercells, where should 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 go?
options: In the four corners and the centre
quiz.explain: Corners and the centre never touch each other, and each touches only edge cells holding 1 to 4.
steps: In a 3 by 3 table, the four corners and the centre never touch each other.
Each of them touches only edge cells.
Put 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 there and 1, 2, 3, 4 on the edges.
Then all five beat their neighbours → 5 supercells.
Answer: In the four corners and the centre
quiz.mistake: Puts big numbers next to each other

quiz.q: Fill the row 4, ?, 6 so that the middle cell is a supercell. Which number works?
quiz.explain: The middle number must beat both 4 and 6, so it must be more than 6: 7.
steps: The middle cell must be bigger than both neighbours, 4 and 6.
So it must be more than 6.
5, 3 and 2 are not more than 6; 7 is.
quiz.mistake: Picks a number between the neighbours

quiz.q: In the table 5 8 1 / 2 6 9, how many supercells are there?
quiz.explain: 8: neighbours 5, 1, 6 → yes. 9: neighbours 1, 6 → yes. 5 (8 bigger), 1, 2, 6 (8 and 9 bigger) → no. So 2.
steps: 8: neighbours 5, 1, 6 → all smaller → supercell. 9: neighbours 1, 6 → supercell.
5 (next to 8), 1 (next to 8, 9), 2 (next to 5, 6), 6 (next to 8, 9) are not.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to check the cell below or above

quiz.q: Raju says: 'In my table no cell is a supercell.' Can he be right?

Yes, if there are no even numbers
Yes, if the table is big
No, the largest number is always a supercell
quiz.explain: With different numbers, the largest one beats all its neighbours, so there is always at least one supercell.
steps: All numbers in the table are different.
The largest number is bigger than every other number, so bigger than all its neighbours.
So the largest number is always a supercell.
Answer: No, the largest number is always a supercell
quiz.mistake: Does not see that the biggest number is always a supercell

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can the tiniest number in my table be a supercell if it sits in a corner?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Its neighbours are all bigger, so the smallest can never be a supercell!

topics.title: Making numbers and reading number lines

learn.hook: With the digits 4, 0, 7, 2 and 9, how big a number can you build? How small?
points: Largest number from given digits: write the digits from largest to smallest: 4, 0, 7, 2, 9 → 97,420.

On a number line, find the scale first: if 0 and 100 are 10 gaps apart, each gap is 10. Then read the marks.

example.q: Using 4, 0, 7, 2, 9 once each, which 5-digit number is closest to 50,000?
steps: Just below 50,000: start with 4, then the largest arrangement of the rest: 49,720.

So 5,400 is largest and the gap is 300.

learn.hook: Numbers have personalities! Some are even, some are odd, some are 'supercells' that tower over their neighbours.
points: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, and even + odd = odd.

Five odd numbers = two pairs (each even) + one odd number left over.

steps: Add the digits of each number.

quiz.explain: Each even number is made of pairs. Putting pairs together still gives only pairs, so the sum is even.
steps: An even number can be split into pairs with nothing left over.
Putting two such numbers together gives only pairs.
So nothing is left over, and the sum is even.
quiz.mistake: Thinks large even numbers might behave differently

learn.hook: Pick almost any 4-digit number, follow a simple recipe, and you will always land on 6174. Spooky? No, it's maths!
points: Take a 4-digit number whose digits are not all the same.
Arrange its digits from largest to smallest, and again from smallest to largest.
Subtract the smaller number from the larger one. Keep zeros: 0378 counts as a 4-digit arrangement.
Repeat with the answer. You always reach 6174 within 7 steps, and 7641 − 1467 = 6174 brings it back to itself.

learn.hook: With only ₹5 and ₹3 coins, can you pay exactly ₹7? Try it!
points: You can build a target by adding chosen numbers again and again: with 5s and 3s, 11 = 5 + 3 + 3. But 7 cannot be made by adding them.
Allowing subtraction makes more targets possible: 7 = 5 + 5 − 3.
Digits and sizes: two 3-digit numbers add to at least 100 + 100 = 200 and at most 999 + 999 = 1998, so the sum is never a 2-digit number.
Always, sometimes or never? The sum of two 4-digit numbers is SOMETIMES a 5-digit number (6000 + 7000 = 13,000, but 1000 + 2000 = 3000).
To find a total quickly, look for groups: 6 rows of 8 coins is 6 × 8 = 48, much faster than counting one by one.

topics.title: Collatz chains and mixed number puzzles

learn.hook: Start with 7 and keep playing Collatz: you'll climb to 52 before you crash down to 1!
points: Collatz rule: even → halve it; odd → multiply by 3 and add 1. Keep going until you reach 1.
From 12: 12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. It reaches 1 after 9 steps.
A power of 2 (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ...) only ever halves, so it falls straight to 1. 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 takes 6 steps.
Once a chain reaches any power of 2, it will drop straight to 1.
Odd-digit puzzles: from 100 to 199, numbers with all digits odd have hundreds digit 1, tens digit 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 and ones digit 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9: 5 × 5 = 25 numbers.

steps: Halving a power of 2 gives a smaller power of 2.

learn.hook: How many times do you blink in a day? You don't need to count all day to find out!
points: We estimate when an exact count is not needed: the crowd at a mela, rice for a party, or time to walk to school.
Exact answers are needed for money change, exam marks and medicine doses.
Estimate big numbers from small ones: if you blink about 15 times a minute, in an hour that is about 15 × 60 = 900 blinks.
A quick 30-second estimate uses easy round numbers: 98 + 203 is about 100 + 200 = 300.

learn.hook: Play the game of 21 with a friend. With one secret, you can win every single time!
points: Game of 21: start at 0. Players take turns adding 1, 2 or 3 to the total. Whoever reaches 21 wins.
Work backwards: if you say 17, your friend can only reach 18, 19 or 20, and then you reach 21. So 17 is a key number.
Going back in 4s, the key numbers are 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21. Go first, say 1, and then always land on the next key number.
Game of 99: players add any number from 1 to 10. Going back in 11s, the key numbers are 11, 22, 33, ..., 88, 99.
In the game of 99, the first player cannot reach 11 in one move, so the second player can always win by landing on the multiples of 11.

example.q: In the game of 21, your friend just made the total 10. What should you add?
steps: The next key number after 10 is 13.

learn.hook: Some puzzles a Class 6 student can understand are so hard that no mathematician in the world has solved them yet!
points: Numbers carry information, make patterns, help us estimate and power many puzzles and games.
A clear list of steps for a task, like Kaprekar's routine or the Collatz rule, is called a procedure (an algorithm). Thinking in such steps is called computational thinking.
Computers follow procedures exactly, so writing good step-by-step rules is how we tell computers what to do.
Some easy-to-say number problems are still unsolved. Nobody has proved that every number reaches 1 in the Collatz game.

example.q: Write a step-by-step procedure for finding the digit sum of any number.
steps: Step 2: Take its digits one by one.
Step 4: The total is the digit sum.

learn.reallife: Recipes, the steps to withdraw money from an ATM and directions to a friend's house are all procedures.
