quiz.q: To draw a face with two eyes and a nose using a compass, which should you draw first?
options: The big circle for the face
quiz.explain: Draw the outline first; then the other circles can be placed inside it.
steps: The eyes and nose must be placed inside the face.
So draw the big outline circle for the face first.
Then place the smaller circles inside it.
Answer: The big circle for the face
quiz.mistake: Starts with small details

quiz.q: An eye shape is made by two arcs bulging in opposite directions. Where do the arcs meet?
options: At the two corners of the eye
quiz.explain: The arcs join at the two pointed corners.
steps: The two arcs bulge in opposite directions.
They start and end at the same two points.
Those are the pointed corners of the eye.
So they meet at the two corners.
Answer: At the two corners of the eye
quiz.mistake: Thinks arcs must cross in the middle

quiz.q: Lata draws a wave of 6 half-circles each of radius 1.5 cm. How long is the wave's base line?
quiz.explain: Diameter = 3 cm; 6 × 3 = 18 cm.
steps: So the base line is 18 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the radius

quiz.q: In a half-circle wave, the half-circles go alternately…
quiz.explain: Alternating up and down makes it look like a wave.
steps: In a wave, one hump goes up and the next goes down.
So the half-circles alternate up and down.
Both up or both down would not look like a wave.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all half-circles face the same way

teach.ask: Gappu wants a wave of 4 half-circles on a 12 cm line. 'What radius should I use?'
teach.praise: Tweet! 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm diameter, so radius 1.5 cm!
teach.nudge: How wide is each half-circle?

revise.summary: Pictures can be built from circles and arcs, like a face with a smile, an eye made of two arcs, or a wave of half-circles. For a wave of n equal half-circles on a line of length L, each diameter is L ÷ n.
focus: Find the radius and centres of half-circles in a wave
Find how many half-circles fit on a line or the length of a wave
Plan a drawing starting with the big circle
remember: Diameter of each half-circle = L ÷ n; radius = half of that
Centres sit at the middle of each piece
4 half-circles on 16 cm: radius 2 cm, centres at 2, 6, 10, 14 cm
traps: Don't give the diameter when the radius is asked
Divide the line by the diameter, not the radius, to count half-circles
Wave half-circles go alternately up and down

learn.hook: Every rectangle has four perfect corners. Let's build one, step by step, and decorate with circles!
points: A rectangle has opposite sides equal and all four angles 90°. A square has all four sides equal and all angles 90°.
To draw a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle: draw AB = 6 cm, make 90° angles at A and B, mark 4 cm up from each end, then join the top points.
The diagonals of a rectangle join opposite corners. They are equal in length and cut each other into halves.
Circles with the same centre but different radii are called concentric circles, like ripples in a pond.
Always check: measure the sides and diagonals after drawing to see if your rectangle is accurate.

example.q: Draw a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm. What should its perimeter be?
steps: At P and Q, draw lines at 90°.
Mark S and R 3 cm up those lines.
Join SR; it should measure 5 cm.
example.answer: A rectangle with sides 5, 3, 5, 3 cm and perimeter 16 cm

learn.reallife: Cricket pitches, carrom boards and doors are rectangles; dartboards and archery targets are concentric circles.

games.title: Match the shape word to its meaning
pairs: All points the same distance from the centre

games.title: Always true for every rectangle?
items: All four angles are 90°
Opposite sides are equal
The two diagonals are equal
The diagonals cut each other into halves
All four sides are equal

Its length is double its breadth
It has only one right angle

quiz.q: Kabir draws a rectangle with one side 7 cm and the next side 4 cm. How long is the side opposite the 7 cm side?
quiz.explain: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so it is 7 cm.
steps: In a rectangle, opposite sides are equal.
The side opposite the 7 cm side is also 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the opposite side equals the next side

quiz.q: How big is each corner angle of a rectangle?
quiz.explain: All four angles of a rectangle are right angles, 90° each.
steps: All four corners of a rectangle are right angles.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a rectangle's corner with a straight angle

quiz.q: One diagonal of a rectangle is 10 cm long. How long is the other diagonal?
quiz.explain: The two diagonals of a rectangle are always equal, so it is 10 cm.
steps: The two diagonals of a rectangle are always equal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the second diagonal is half or double the first

quiz.q: The diagonals of rectangle ABCD meet at O. If AC = 12 cm, how long is AO?
quiz.explain: The diagonals cut each other into halves, so AO = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that O is the middle of AC

quiz.q: Aisha draws circles with the same centre and radii 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. What are these circles called?
quiz.explain: Circles that share a centre are concentric circles.
steps: All three circles share one centre.
Circles with the same centre are concentric circles.
Their radii differ, so they are not equal circles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks circles with the same centre must be equal

quiz.q: Which steps draw a square of side 5 cm?
options: Draw two 5 cm lines anywhere and join them
Draw a circle of radius 5 cm
Draw a 5 cm line and a 10 cm line at 90°
Draw a 5 cm line, make 90° angles at both ends, mark 5 cm up each, then join
quiz.explain: A square needs four 5 cm sides and four right angles. The last set of steps gives exactly that.
steps: A square needs four sides of 5 cm and four right angles.
Draw a 5 cm base, make 90° at both ends, mark 5 cm up each, and join.
That gives exactly four 5 cm sides and four 90° corners.
So the last set of steps.
Answer: Draw a 5 cm line, make 90° angles at both ends, mark 5 cm up each, then join
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the corners must be right angles

quiz.q: Harpreet draws a circle of radius 3 cm. She draws a second circle of radius 3 cm whose centre lies on the first circle. How far apart are the two centres?
quiz.explain: The second centre is on the first circle, so it is one radius, 3 cm, from the first centre.
steps: The second centre lies on the first circle.
Every point on the first circle is 3 cm (one radius) from its centre.
So the two centres are 3 cm apart.
quiz.mistake: Adds both radii (6 cm)

quiz.q: Joseph wants to draw a rectangle with perimeter 20 cm and one side 6 cm. Which pair of side lengths should he use?
quiz.explain: Length + breadth = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 cm, so the other side is 10 − 6 = 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 6 from 20 without halving (14 cm)

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a rectangle for his nest door: 'How do I make sure it's a real rectangle?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Measure with a ruler, make 90° corners, keep opposite sides equal. A perfect door!
teach.nudge: What must the corners be, and which sides have to be equal?

revise.summary: A rectangle has opposite sides equal and all angles 90°; a square has all sides equal and all angles 90°. A rectangle's diagonals are equal and cut each other into halves, and circles with the same centre are concentric.
focus: Draw a rectangle or square of given sides using 90° angles
Use the diagonal facts: equal and cut each other into halves
Know concentric circles
Find side lengths from the perimeter
remember: Rectangle: opposite sides equal, all four angles 90°
Diagonals of a rectangle are equal and cut each other into halves
Concentric circles: same centre, different radii
traps: The side opposite 7 cm is 7 cm, not the next side's length
Halve the perimeter before subtracting: perimeter 20, side 6 → other side 4
Circles with the same centre need not be equal

topics.title: Naming and spotting squares and rectangles

learn.hook: Turn a square on its corner and it looks like a diamond. Is it still a square?
points: Name a quadrilateral by its corners in order around it: ABCD means A to B to C to D and back to A. ABDC would be a different (crossed) path.
In square ABCD, side AB is next to BC, and AB is opposite CD.
A tilted square or rectangle is still a square or rectangle: tilting doesn't change side lengths or angles.
On dot paper, a tilted square can be drawn by going, for example, 2 right and 1 up, then 1 left and 2 up, and so on. Check that all sides are equal and all angles are right angles.

example.q: On dot paper, from A go 3 right and 1 up to B, then 1 left and 3 up to C, then 3 left and 1 down to D. Is ABCD a square?
steps: Each side uses a '3 and 1' step, so all sides are equal.
Each turn is a quarter turn, so all angles are 90°.
Yes, ABCD is a tilted square.

learn.reallife: Floor tiles laid diagonally and kites flown on their corner are still squares, just turned.

games.title: Tilted shapes
items: A square turned on its corner is still a square.
Sides and angles do not change.
Rectangle ABCD and rectangle ACBD name the same path.
ACBD goes corner to corner across.
In square PQRS, PQ is opposite RS.
They do not share a corner.
A tilted rectangle has angles other than 90°.
Turning keeps the angles.
On dot paper, a tilted square needs equal sides and right angles.
That is how to check it.

quiz.q: Which name correctly goes around the quadrilateral with corners P, Q, R, S in order?
quiz.explain: Corners must be listed in order around the shape: PQRS.
steps: Corners must be named in order going round the shape.
P → Q → R → S is the order around it.
PRQS, PSQR and QSPR jump across the shape.
quiz.mistake: Lists the corners in random order

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD, which side is opposite AB?
quiz.explain: AB and CD do not share a corner; they are opposite.
steps: In ABCD the corners go A, B, C, D in order.
AB and CD do not share a corner.
BC and DA share a corner with AB; AC is a diagonal.
quiz.mistake: Picks a neighbouring side

quiz.q: A square is turned so it stands on one corner. What are its angles?
quiz.explain: Turning a shape does not change its angles.
steps: Turning a shape does not change its angles.
So the turned square still has four 90° angles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the tilted look changes the angles

quiz.q: In square WXYZ, which pair of sides are next to each other (adjacent)?
quiz.explain: XY and YZ share the corner Y.
steps: XY and YZ share the corner Y.
WX and YZ, XY and ZW are opposite; WY and XZ are diagonals.
quiz.mistake: Picks opposite sides

quiz.q: On dot paper, a tilted square has one side going 2 right and 1 up. What must the next side do?
quiz.explain: Turning a quarter turn: '2 right, 1 up' becomes '1 left, 2 up'.
steps: In a tilted square the next side is the first side turned a quarter turn.
'2 right, 1 up' turned a quarter turn becomes '1 left, 2 up'.
This keeps the side the same length and at a right angle.
quiz.mistake: Repeats the same step

quiz.q: Which statement about a tilted rectangle is true?
options: Its opposite sides are still equal
quiz.explain: Tilting keeps all lengths and angles.
steps: Tilting a rectangle only turns it.
Turning keeps all lengths and angles the same.
So its opposite sides are still equal.
It does not become a square or curved.
Answer: Its opposite sides are still equal
quiz.mistake: Thinks tilting changes the shape

quiz.q: On dot paper, Kiran draws a shape with sides of steps '2 right 1 up', '1 left 2 up', '2 left 1 down', '1 right 2 down'. What has she drawn?
quiz.explain: All four sides use the same 2-and-1 step, turned by quarter turns: a tilted square.
steps: All four sides use the same 2-and-1 step.
Each side is a quarter turn of the one before.
Equal sides with right-angle turns make a square.
So she has drawn a tilted square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only upright shapes are squares

quiz.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, AC joins…
quiz.explain: A and C are not next to each other, so AC is a diagonal joining opposite corners.
steps: In ABCD, A is next to B and D, not to C.
So A and C are opposite corners.
AC joins them; it is a diagonal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks AC is a side

teach.ask: Gappu turns his square cracker on its corner. 'Now it's a diamond, not a square!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Turning doesn't change it: equal sides, right angles. Still a square!
teach.nudge: Did the side lengths or angles change when you turned it?

revise.summary: A quadrilateral is named by its corners in order around it, so ABCD goes A to B to C to D. A tilted square or rectangle is still a square or rectangle, and tilted squares can be drawn on dot paper.
focus: Name quadrilaterals in order; find adjacent and opposite sides
Know that tilting doesn't change side lengths or angles
Draw and check tilted squares on dot paper
remember: ABCD: A to B to C to D and back to A
In square ABCD, AB is next to BC and opposite CD
Tilted square on dot paper: e.g. 2 right 1 up, then 1 left 2 up, ...
traps: Don't list the corners in random order
Tilting does not change the angles: still all 90°
On dot paper, the next side is not the same step repeated

topics.title: Rectangles: reasons and breaking into squares

learn.hook: Four right angles force the opposite sides to be equal. Can you see why?
points: If a four-sided figure has all four angles 90°, its opposite sides must be equal: it is a rectangle.
Reason: the two sides standing on the base are both perpendicular to it, so the top side stays the same distance from the base all along, and the top is as long as the base.
Points P on side AB and Q on the opposite side DC: the distance PQ is shortest when PQ is perpendicular to the sides. Then PQ equals the other side length of the rectangle.
A rectangle made of 2 identical squares in a row is twice as long as it is wide; of 3 squares, three times as long.

example.q: A rectangle is made of 3 identical squares in a row. Its length is 15 cm. Find its width and perimeter.

learn.reallife: Doors and windows are made with four right angles, so their opposite edges match and they fit their frames.

items.q: 2 squares of side 6 cm: rectangle length
3 squares of side 4 cm: rectangle length
Rectangle 20 cm long of 4 squares: square side

games.title: Right-angle reasoning
items: A four-sided figure with four right angles has equal opposite sides.
It must be a rectangle.
PQ between opposite sides AB and DC is shortest when it is perpendicular to them.
Then it equals the width.
A rectangle of 2 identical squares is a square.
It is twice as long as wide.
Every rectangle can be cut into identical squares as wide as the rectangle.
Only if the length is a whole multiple of the width.
If PQ is slanted, it is longer than the width.
Slanting makes the path longer.

quiz.q: A rectangle is made of 2 identical squares placed side by side. Its width is 7 cm. What is its length?
quiz.explain: Length = 2 × 7 = 14 cm.
steps: Two identical squares side by side, each of side 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is a square

quiz.q: A rectangle 24 cm long is made of 3 identical squares in a row. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Side = 8 cm. Perimeter = 2 × (24 + 8) = 64 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the perimeters of the squares

quiz.q: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 10 cm and BC = 6 cm. P moves on AB and Q moves on DC. What is the shortest possible PQ?
quiz.explain: PQ is shortest when it is perpendicular, and then it equals BC = 6 cm.
steps: P is on AB and Q is on DC, the two 10 cm sides.
The shortest PQ goes straight across, perpendicular to both.
So the shortest PQ is 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the long side

quiz.q: In that rectangle (10 cm × 6 cm), can PQ ever be shorter than 6 cm?
options: Yes, if P is at a corner
Only if the rectangle is tilted
Yes, if Q is in the middle
quiz.explain: Any slanted PQ is longer than the straight-across distance of 6 cm.
steps: The straight-across distance between AB and DC is 6 cm.
Any slanted PQ is longer than this.
So PQ can never be less than 6 cm.
Answer: No, 6 cm is the shortest
quiz.mistake: Thinks moving to a corner shortens it

quiz.q: A four-sided figure has angles 90°, 90°, 90° and 90°. One side is 9 cm and the next is 5 cm. What is the perimeter?
quiz.explain: Four right angles mean a rectangle: 2 × (9 + 5) = 28 cm.
steps: Four right angles make a rectangle, so opposite sides are equal.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two sides

quiz.q: Why must a figure with four right angles have equal opposite sides?
options: The two sides on the base are both perpendicular, so the top stays parallel and matches the base
Because all sides are always equal
quiz.explain: Perpendicular sides at both ends keep the top the same distance from the base.
steps: Both sides standing on the base are perpendicular to it.
So the top stays the same distance from the base all along (parallel).
Then the top matches the base and the two upright sides match each other.
Answer: The two sides on the base are both perpendicular, so the top stays parallel and matches the base
quiz.mistake: Thinks four right angles mean four equal sides

quiz.q: A rectangle 18 cm × 6 cm. How many 6 cm squares can it be broken into?
quiz.explain: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 squares.
steps: The rectangle is 6 cm wide, so each square has side 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides 18 by 3

quiz.q: Can a 10 cm × 4 cm rectangle be broken into identical squares of side 4 cm with nothing left?
options: No, 10 is not a multiple of 4
quiz.explain: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, so a strip would be left over.
steps: Squares of side 4 cm along the 10 cm side: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5.
So a 2 cm strip would be left over.
Answer: No, 10 is not a multiple of 4
quiz.mistake: Thinks any rectangle can be split into squares

teach.ask: Gappu has a rectangle made of 2 identical square tiles. It is 8 cm long. 'How wide is it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Each square is 4 cm, so the rectangle is 4 cm wide!
teach.nudge: How long is each square's side?

revise.summary: If a four-sided figure has all four angles 90°, its opposite sides must be equal, so it is a rectangle. The shortest distance between opposite sides is along a perpendicular, and rectangles made of identical squares are 2 or 3 times as long as they are wide.
focus: Explain why four right angles give equal opposite sides
Find the shortest distance between opposite sides
Work with rectangles made of identical squares
remember: Four angles of 90° → opposite sides equal: a rectangle
Shortest PQ between opposite sides: PQ perpendicular to the sides, equal to the other side length
2 squares in a row: length = 2 × width; 3 squares: length = 3 × width
traps: Four right angles don't mean four equal sides
Don't add the squares' perimeters to get the rectangle's perimeter
Not every rectangle splits into identical squares: 10 × 4 does not

learn.hook: Draw a square inside a rectangle, squares that look like they're falling, and a square full of holes!
points: Always make a rough sketch first. Mark the lengths and right angles you know, then plan the order of steps.
Square inside a rectangle: in a 10 cm × 6 cm rectangle, a 6 cm square fits touching three sides, leaving a 4 cm × 6 cm strip.
Falling squares: draw squares of the same size, each one tilted a little more, using a protractor for the tilt angle.
A square with holes: draw the square, then circles at chosen centres; check each circle stays inside by comparing radius and distances to the sides.

example.q: A 6 cm square has a circular hole at its centre. What is the largest radius the hole can have and still fit inside?
steps: The centre is 3 cm from every side.
A circle of radius 3 cm just touches all four sides.
So the largest radius is 3 cm.

learn.reallife: Architects sketch by hand before drawing exact plans, and tailors chalk rough outlines before cutting.

items.q: Largest square in a 10 by 6 rectangle: side

Largest circle in a 6 cm square: radius
Largest circle in an 8 cm square: diameter
Two 5 cm squares side by side: total length

quiz.q: What is the largest square that fits inside a 12 cm × 7 cm rectangle?
quiz.explain: The square's side cannot exceed the shorter side, 7 cm.
steps: The square must fit inside both directions.
Its side cannot be more than the shorter side, 7 cm.
So the largest square has side 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the longer side

quiz.q: After cutting that 7 cm square from the 12 cm × 7 cm rectangle, what is left?
quiz.explain: 12 − 7 = 5, so a 5 cm × 7 cm strip remains.
steps: The rectangle is 12 cm × 7 cm; the square takes 7 cm of the length.
So a 5 cm × 7 cm rectangle is left.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from the wrong side

quiz.q: Why should you draw a rough sketch before constructing?
options: Because it is the final answer
To plan the steps and see where lengths go
quiz.explain: Sketches help plan before the exact drawing.
steps: A rough sketch is drawn before the exact construction.
It helps plan the steps and see where each length goes.
It is not the final answer and does not replace the ruler.
Answer: To plan the steps and see where lengths go
quiz.mistake: Thinks sketches are a waste of time

quiz.q: A circle of radius 2 cm is drawn with its centre 3 cm from the edge of a square. Does the circle stay inside (on that side)?
quiz.explain: The circle reaches 2 cm from its centre, which is 3 cm from the edge, so it stays inside.
steps: The circle reaches 2 cm from its centre in every direction.
The centre is 3 cm from the edge.
2 < 3, so the circle stops 1 cm before the edge.
quiz.mistake: Compares diameter with distance incorrectly

quiz.q: In a 10 cm square, the largest circle that fits has diameter…
quiz.explain: It touches all four sides, so diameter = 10 cm.
steps: The largest circle in a square touches all four sides.
So its diameter equals the side of the square.
quiz.mistake: Uses the radius

quiz.q: For 'falling squares', each square is tilted 15° more than the one before. The first is not tilted. How much is the 4th tilted?
quiz.mistake: Starts counting from 15°

quiz.q: Shalini sketches a rectangle with a square inside it, touching three sides. The rectangle is 9 cm × 4 cm. What is the square's side?
quiz.explain: It touches the two long sides, so its side equals the width, 4 cm.
steps: The square touches three sides, including both long sides.
So the square's side equals the distance between the long sides.
So the square's side is 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the length

quiz.q: Two 3 cm square holes are cut from a 10 cm × 10 cm square card. What area of card is left?
steps: Each hole = 3 × 3 = 9 cm²; two holes = 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only one hole

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a square inside his 8 cm × 5 cm rectangular nest box. 'How big can it be?'
teach.praise: Tweet! As big as the shorter side: 5 cm. A sketch helps you see it!
teach.nudge: Which side of the box limits the square?

revise.summary: Always make a rough sketch first, marking known lengths and right angles, then plan the steps. Challenges include fitting squares and circles inside shapes and drawing tilted 'falling squares'.
focus: Use a rough sketch to plan a construction
Find the largest square or circle that fits inside a shape
Check that a circle stays inside by comparing radius and distance to the sides
Find tilt angles and leftover areas
remember: Largest square in a 10 cm × 6 cm rectangle: 6 cm, leaving a 4 cm × 6 cm strip
A circle stays inside if its radius is less than the distance from its centre to each side
Largest circle in a 6 cm square: radius 3 cm
traps: The largest square uses the shorter side, not the longer
Compare the radius (not the diameter) with the distance to the edge
For falling squares, the first is not tilted, so the 4th is tilted 3 × 15° = 45°

topics.title: Diagonals and the angles they make

learn.hook: Draw a diagonal in a rectangle and two corner angles split. Do the pieces always add to 90°?
points: A diagonal splits each corner angle it passes through into two parts that add up to 90°.
In rectangle ABCD with diagonal AC: ∠BAC = ∠ACD and ∠CAD = ∠ACB. The diagonal makes equal pairs of angles.
In a square, a diagonal splits each corner exactly in half: 45° and 45°.
Rectangle from diagonal angles: if the diagonal makes 30° with AB, draw AB, draw a 30° ray at A, a perpendicular at B; where they cross is C. Then complete the rectangle.
Rectangle from a side and a diagonal: draw AB, a perpendicular at B, then an arc from A with radius equal to the diagonal; it cuts the perpendicular at C.

example.q: In rectangle ABCD, diagonal AC makes ∠BAC = 35°. Find ∠CAD and ∠ACD.

learn.reallife: Carpenters check a frame is a true rectangle by measuring both diagonals: if they match, the corners are square.

items.q: Square: each part of the corner

games.title: Rectangle from a side and a diagonal
items: Draw side AB
Draw a perpendicular to AB at B
With centre A and radius equal to the diagonal, cut the perpendicular at C
Measure BC
Mark D above A so that AD = BC, and join CD

quiz.q: In rectangle PQRS, diagonal PR makes ∠QPR = 28°. What is ∠RPS?
quiz.explain: The two parts add to 90°: 90 − 28 = 62°.
steps: Corner P of the rectangle is 90°.
The diagonal splits it into ∠QPR and ∠RPS.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the diagonal halves the angle

quiz.q: In square ABCD, what angle does diagonal AC make with side AB?
quiz.explain: A square's diagonal splits the 90° corner into 45° and 45°.
steps: Each corner of a square is 90°.
The diagonal of a square splits the corner into two equal parts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the diagonal makes 60°

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD with ∠BAC = 50°, what is ∠ACD?
quiz.explain: ∠ACD = ∠BAC: the diagonal makes equal pairs of angles.
steps: AB and CD are opposite, parallel sides; AC crosses both.
The diagonal makes equal angles with the opposite sides: ∠ACD = ∠BAC.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 90 wrongly

quiz.q: A diagonal of a rectangle splits a corner angle into two parts. Which pair of parts is impossible?
quiz.explain: The two parts must add to 90°, so 60° and 40° (100°) is impossible.
steps: The two parts make up the 90° corner, so they must add to 90°.
quiz.mistake: Does not check that the parts add to 90°

quiz.q: To construct a rectangle where the diagonal makes 30° with AB = 6 cm, what do you draw at B?
quiz.explain: BC must be perpendicular to AB; the 30° ray from A meets it at C.
steps: In a rectangle, BC must be perpendicular to AB.
So draw a 90° line at B.
The 30° ray from A meets this line at C.
So draw a perpendicular at B.
quiz.mistake: Draws the 30° ray at B

quiz.q: To draw a rectangle with AB = 4 cm and diagonal AC = 5 cm, what compass opening cuts the perpendicular at B?
quiz.explain: The arc is drawn from A with radius equal to the diagonal, 5 cm.
steps: C must be on the perpendicular at B and 5 cm from A (AC is the diagonal).
So draw an arc from A with radius 5 cm.
Where it cuts the perpendicular is C.
quiz.mistake: Uses the side length

quiz.q: In that rectangle (AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm), BC measures 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.mistake: Includes the diagonal

quiz.q: Is a rectangle's diagonal always the bisector of the corner angle?
options: Only when the rectangle is a square
quiz.explain: Only in a square are the two parts equal (45° each).
steps: A diagonal bisects a corner only if it splits 90° into 45° and 45°.
That happens only when all sides are equal.
A rectangle with equal sides is a square.
So only when the rectangle is a square.
Answer: Only when the rectangle is a square
quiz.mistake: Thinks every diagonal bisects the corner

teach.ask: Gappu draws a diagonal in his rectangle and one part of the corner is 25°. 'What's the other part?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The parts add to 90°, so the other is 65°!
teach.nudge: What do the two parts of the corner add to?

revise.summary: A diagonal splits each corner angle of a rectangle into two parts that add up to 90°, and makes equal pairs of angles. In a square it splits each corner exactly in half, 45° and 45°.
focus: Find angles made by a rectangle's diagonal using the 90° total and equal pairs
Construct a rectangle from a side and a diagonal angle
Construct a rectangle from a side and a diagonal length
remember: Parts of a corner split by a diagonal add up to 90°
In rectangle ABCD: ∠BAC = ∠ACD and ∠CAD = ∠ACB
In a square, a diagonal makes 45° and 45°
traps: A rectangle's diagonal does not halve the corner unless it is a square
Check that the two parts add to 90° (60° and 40° is impossible)
Don't include the diagonal in the perimeter

topics.title: Equal-sided figures: a house and a rhombus

learn.hook: Can you draw a house where every edge is the same length, using only a compass and ruler?
points: To find a point at the same distance from two points A and B, draw arcs of equal radius from A and from B. Where they cross is the point.
House with all sides equal: draw a square of side 5 cm, then from the two top corners draw arcs of radius 5 cm. They meet at the roof tip, making an equilateral triangle on top.
The roof triangle has all sides 5 cm, so each roof angle is 60°.
A rhombus has 4 equal sides but need not have right angles. Draw AB, then from A draw an arc; pick D on it at any angle, then arcs from B and D of the same radius meet at C.

learn.hook: A butterfly, a rangoli and the Taj Mahal share a secret: their parts repeat in a perfect pattern!
points: Symmetry means parts of a figure repeat in a definite pattern.
In mirror symmetry, one half is the mirror image of the other, like a butterfly's wings.
In turning symmetry, a part repeats as you turn around a centre, like the petals of a flower or the pattern of a rangoli.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature (leaves, butterflies, snowflakes), art (rangoli, kolam) and buildings (the Taj Mahal, temple gopurams).

example.q: Why do we say the front of the Taj Mahal is symmetric?
steps: Imagine a vertical line through the middle of the main dome.
The left half (minarets, arches) matches the right half exactly, like a mirror image.
So its parts repeat in a definite pattern: it has symmetry.
example.answer: Its left and right halves are mirror images

learn.reallife: Designers use symmetry in sarees, logos and jewellery because our eyes find it balanced and beautiful.

learn.hook: Fold a butterfly picture down the middle and both wings match perfectly. That's line symmetry!
points: A shape has line symmetry if you can fold it along a line so that the two halves match exactly.
The fold line is called the line of symmetry (or axis of symmetry). Each half is a mirror image of the other.
Some shapes have many lines of symmetry: a rectangle has 2, an equilateral triangle 3, a square 4 and a circle has unlimited lines.
A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry. A regular hexagon has 6.
Capital letters: A and M have a vertical line, B and E a horizontal line, H and X have both, and F, G, J and R have none.

example.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?
steps: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides.
Each line of symmetry goes through one corner and the middle of the opposite side.

learn.reallife: The Taj Mahal, rangoli designs, leaves and many temple doors are symmetrical.

steps: Fold a circle along any line through its centre.

Answer: No, every line through the centre is a line of symmetry
quiz.mistake: Counts only the vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines

learn.hook: Put a mirror on the line and the picture completes itself!
points: In reflection symmetry each point has a mirror image on the other side of the line, at the same distance from it.
A point 3 squares to the left of a vertical line of symmetry has its image 3 squares to the right, in the same row.
Not every fold is a line of symmetry: a diagonal of a non-square rectangle is NOT a line of symmetry, because the folded triangles don't sit exactly on each other.
To complete a figure on squared paper, reflect each corner point across the line, then join the image points in the same order.

example.q: On squared paper, the line of symmetry is vertical. Point P is 2 squares left of it and 4 squares up. Where is its image?
steps: Stay in the same row: 4 squares up.
Go to the other side, the same distance: 2 squares right of the line.
The image is 2 right of the line, 4 up.

learn.reallife: Lakes reflect mountains, and a dressing mirror shows your mirror image: same distance behind the mirror as you are in front.

topics.title: Making symmetric shapes: blots, folds and cuts

learn.hook: Drop ink, fold, press, open: you've made a perfect butterfly!
points: Ink blot: put a few drops of paint on one side of a fold, press the paper, open it: the blot is symmetric about the fold.
Fold and cut: cut a shape along a folded edge, and the opened shape is symmetric about the fold line.
Punching a hole through a folded paper makes two holes, mirror images across the fold.
Folding twice (in half, then in half again) and cutting gives a shape with 2 lines of symmetry. A hole punched through gives 4 holes.

learn.hook: Some triangles have 3 lines of symmetry, some have 1, and some have none!
points: An equilateral triangle (all sides equal) has 3 lines of symmetry: from each corner to the middle of the opposite side.
An isosceles triangle (exactly two sides equal) has 1 line of symmetry: from the corner between the equal sides to the middle of the opposite side.
A scalene triangle (all sides different) has no line of symmetry.
A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry: 3 through opposite corners and 3 through the middles of opposite sides.

example.q: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
steps: Two sides are equal (5 cm), the third is different.
It has 1 line of symmetry, from the corner between the 5 cm sides to the middle of the 8 cm side.

So it goes from that corner to the middle of the opposite side.

quiz.mistake: Picks a line along a side

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
quiz.explain: 3 through opposite corners and 3 through the middles of opposite sides.
steps: 3 lines go through the middles of opposite sides.
So a regular hexagon has 6 lines.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the corner-to-corner lines

quiz.q: A triangle has exactly one line of symmetry. What can it be?
quiz.explain: Exactly one line means exactly two equal sides.
steps: Exactly one line of symmetry means exactly two equal sides.
That is an isosceles triangle that is not equilateral.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the triangle types

quiz.q: Can a triangle have exactly 2 lines of symmetry?
quiz.explain: If it has two, it must have three equal sides and so 3 lines.
steps: 0 lines: scalene; 1 line: isosceles; 3 lines: equilateral.
If a triangle had 2 lines, all three sides would be equal, giving 3 lines.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any number is possible

quiz.q: A road sign is an equilateral triangle. How many ways can it be folded so the halves match?
quiz.explain: An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry.
steps: The sign is an equilateral triangle.
An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry.
So it can be folded 3 ways.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the vertical fold

teach.ask: Gappu has a triangle with sides 4, 4 and 6. 'How many ways can I fold it so halves match?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Two equal sides make it isosceles: just 1 line of symmetry!
teach.nudge: How many of its sides are equal?

revise.summary: An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry, an isosceles triangle has 1 and a scalene triangle has none. A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry.
focus: Count lines of symmetry of a triangle from its side lengths
Locate the line of symmetry of an isosceles triangle
Know the hexagon's 6 lines (through corners and through side middles)
remember: Equilateral: 3 lines (each corner to the middle of the opposite side)
Isosceles: 1 line (from the corner between the equal sides to the middle of the opposite side)
Scalene: no line of symmetry
traps: Not every triangle has 3 lines, or even 1
A triangle cannot have exactly 2 lines of symmetry: it has 0, 1 or 3
A hexagon's lines include 3 through side middles, not just corner-to-corner

learn.hook: Spin a pinwheel a little and it looks just the same. That's rotational symmetry!
points: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same after a turn of less than a full turn about its centre.
The smallest such turn is the smallest angle of symmetry. For a square it is 90°.
A square matches itself at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°: 4 times in one full turn.
Smallest angle × number of matches = 360°. For an equilateral triangle: 120° × 3 = 360°.
The Ashoka Chakra on our flag has 24 equal spokes, so its smallest angle of symmetry is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°.

example.q: A pinwheel has 4 identical blades. What is its smallest angle of rotational symmetry?
steps: The blades are evenly spaced around a full turn of 360°.

learn.reallife: Ceiling fans, bicycle wheels, flowers and many rangoli patterns have rotational symmetry.

Smallest angle of symmetry: wheel with 8 evenly spaced spokes

quiz.q: What is the smallest angle of rotational symmetry of a square?
quiz.explain: A square looks the same after a quarter turn: 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.

quiz.q: A ceiling fan has 3 identical, evenly spaced blades. What is the smallest turn that makes it look the same?

quiz.explain: 360° ÷ 45° = 8 matches in a full turn.
quiz.mistake: Writes the angle itself (45) or halves the answer (4)

quiz.q: Which shape looks the same after a 180° turn but NOT after a 90° turn?
options: A rectangle that is not a square
quiz.explain: A rectangle swaps its long and short sides after 90°, so it doesn't match, but after 180° it does.
steps: A square, triangle and circle match after a 90° turn or less (or never fail).
A non-square rectangle swaps its long and short sides after 90°, so it does not match.
So the rectangle that is not a square.
Answer: A rectangle that is not a square
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a square matches at 90° too

quiz.q: A regular hexagon is turned about its centre. What is the smallest angle that makes it look the same?
quiz.explain: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides: 360° ÷ 6 = 60°.
steps: A regular hexagon has 6 equal parts around its centre.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 (120°) or by 12 (30°)

quiz.q: Kabir's bicycle wheel has 12 identical, evenly spaced spokes. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of spokes as the angle (12°)

quiz.q: Which of these has NO rotational symmetry (except a full turn)?
quiz.explain: F looks different after any turn less than 360°. S looks the same after a half turn (180°).
steps: S looks the same after a half turn (180°).
A square and a circle also have rotational symmetry.
F looks different after any turn less than 360°.
So F has no rotational symmetry.
quiz.mistake: Thinks S has no symmetry because it has no line of symmetry

quiz.q: Joseph says every shape with a line of symmetry also has rotational symmetry. Is he right?
options: No: the letter A has a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry
quiz.explain: Fold A down the middle and the halves match, but turn A and it looks different until a full turn.
steps: Look for a shape with a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry.
The letter A: fold down the middle and the halves match.
Turn A and it looks different until a full turn.
Answer: No: the letter A has a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry
quiz.mistake: Mixes up line symmetry and rotational symmetry

quiz.q: After its first step, the Koch snowflake looks like a six-pointed star. What is its smallest angle of rotational symmetry?
quiz.explain: The star has 6 identical points, so it matches itself every 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. Its order of rotational symmetry is 6.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 3 sides of the starting triangle

teach.ask: Gappu spins a flower with 5 petals: 'What is rotational symmetry, and how do I find its angle?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Turn it until it looks the same again: 360° ÷ 5 = 72°. My flower has rotational symmetry!
teach.nudge: How far do I turn it before it looks the same, and how do I work that angle out?

revise.summary: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same after a turn of less than a full turn about its centre. The smallest such turn is the smallest angle of symmetry, and smallest angle × number of matches = 360°.
focus: Find the smallest angle of symmetry for shapes with equal parts
Find how many times a shape matches itself in a full turn
Tell rotational symmetry apart from line symmetry
remember: Square: smallest angle 90°; matches at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°
Smallest angle × number of matches = 360° (120° × 3 for an equilateral triangle)
Ashoka Chakra: 360° ÷ 24 = 15°
traps: Don't use the number of spokes as the angle: 12 spokes give 30°
A line of symmetry does not mean rotational symmetry (letter A)
S has rotational symmetry even though it has no line of symmetry

topics.title: Centre of rotation and angles of symmetry

learn.hook: A pinwheel spins around one fixed point. That point is the secret to its symmetry!
points: The centre of rotation is the fixed point a figure turns about.
For figures with radial arms (like spokes or fan blades), the arrangement of the arms decides the angles of symmetry. 4 equally spaced arms → 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
If arms are not equally spaced, the figure may only match at 360°: arms pointing up, right and down (no left arm) match only after a full turn.
All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest one, and the smallest one divides 360° exactly.
So a figure can't have a smallest angle of symmetry of 70°, because 70 does not divide 360.

example.q: A figure has 5 identical, equally spaced arms. List its angles of symmetry.

learn.reallife: A wheel turns about its axle (the centre of rotation), and fan blades spread evenly so the fan looks the same as it spins.

Order if the smallest angle is 45°
Order if the smallest angle is 120°

quiz.q: A wheel has 10 equally spaced spokes. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

quiz.q: A figure's smallest angle of symmetry is 60°. Which of these is also an angle of symmetry?
quiz.explain: Angles of symmetry are multiples of 60°: 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°.
steps: All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest one, 60°.
240 = 4 × 60 is in the list; 90, 150, 100 are not.
quiz.mistake: Picks any angle bigger than 60°

quiz.q: Which can NOT be the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure?
quiz.explain: 360 ÷ 50 is not a whole number, so 50° can't be the smallest angle.
steps: The smallest angle must divide 360 exactly.
So 50° cannot be the smallest angle.
quiz.mistake: Does not check if it divides 360

quiz.q: A figure has arms pointing up, right and down only (equal lengths). What is its order of rotational symmetry?
quiz.explain: Turning 90° or 180° moves an arm to the empty left side. It matches only after 360°: order 1.
steps: Arms point up, right and down; left is empty.
Turning 90° or 180° moves an arm into the empty left side, so it does not match.
It matches only after a full 360° turn.
quiz.mistake: Counts arms instead of checking turns

quiz.q: Where is the centre of rotation of a ceiling fan?
options: At the middle where the blades join
quiz.explain: The blades turn about the middle point.
steps: The blades turn about one fixed point.
That point is the middle, where the blades join.
So that is the centre of rotation.
Answer: At the middle where the blades join
quiz.mistake: Picks a point that moves

quiz.q: A rangoli has 8 equal petals. How many angles of symmetry does it have in a full turn (including 360°)?
quiz.explain: Smallest angle 45°, and 360 ÷ 45 = 8 angles.
quiz.mistake: Gives the angle instead of the count

quiz.q: A figure has angles of symmetry 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. What is the smallest?
quiz.explain: The smallest angle of symmetry is 90°, and the others are its multiples.
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest

quiz.q: A logo has 3 identical arms spaced 120° apart. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
quiz.mistake: Thinks a 3-armed figure has order 6

teach.ask: Gappu sees a star with 6 equal points. 'Which turns make it look the same?'
teach.praise: Tweet! 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300° and 360°: all multiples of 60°!
teach.nudge: What is 360 divided by 6?

revise.summary: The centre of rotation is the fixed point a figure turns about, and the arrangement of its arms decides its angles of symmetry. All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest one, which divides 360° exactly.
focus: List all angles of symmetry for equally spaced arms
Find the order of rotational symmetry
Check whether an angle can be a smallest angle of symmetry
remember: Centre of rotation: the fixed point a figure turns about
All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest, which divides 360° exactly
traps: Count turns, not arms: arms up, right and down only have order 1
70° or 50° can't be a smallest angle of symmetry: they don't divide 360
Don't give the angle when the number of matches is asked

topics.title: Circles, coloured sectors and tile designs

learn.hook: A circle is the champion of symmetry: it matches itself after ANY turn!
points: A circle looks the same after a turn of any angle about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
Colouring sectors can control the order: a circle cut into 8 equal sectors with every other sector coloured has order 4 (it matches every 90°).
With 8 sectors, colouring two opposite sectors (like 1 and 5) gives order 2; colouring just one gives order 1.
Tile designs: arrange square tiles with patterns to get exactly one or exactly two lines of symmetry. Check each possible fold line one by one.

example.q: A circle is cut into 6 equal sectors. Sectors 1 and 4 are coloured. What is the order of rotational symmetry?
steps: The coloured sectors are opposite each other (3 apart).
A half turn (180°) moves sector 1 to 4 and 4 to 1: the same look.
A 60° or 120° turn does not match, so the order is 2.

learn.reallife: Wheels, coins and plates are round so they look and work the same however they are turned.

games.title: Circle facts
items: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry.
Folding along it matches the halves.
A circle has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.
It has endlessly many.
A circle looks the same after a 37° turn.
Any turn works for a circle.
Colouring every other sector of 8 gives order 2.
It gives order 4 (every 90°).
A tile design can have exactly one line of symmetry.

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
quiz.explain: Every diameter is a line of symmetry, and there are endlessly many diameters.
steps: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry.
A circle has endlessly many diameters.
So it has endlessly many lines of symmetry.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer is 4 like a square

quiz.q: Which turn makes a circle look the same?
quiz.explain: Every angle is an angle of symmetry of a circle.
steps: A circle looks the same however much it is turned about its centre.
So every angle is an angle of symmetry.
It is not limited to 90°, 180° or 360°.
quiz.mistake: Applies a polygon's rule

quiz.q: A circle has 8 equal sectors; sectors 1, 3, 5, 7 are coloured. What is the order of rotational symmetry?
quiz.explain: A 90° turn shifts by 2 sectors and keeps the pattern. 360 ÷ 90 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Thinks colouring half gives order 2

quiz.q: A circle has 8 equal sectors; only sectors 1 and 5 are coloured. What is the order?
quiz.explain: Only a 180° (or 360°) turn keeps the pattern: order 2.
steps: A 90° turn moves colour to sectors 3 and 7 → no match.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two coloured parts means order 4

quiz.q: A circle has 6 equal sectors. Which colouring gives order 3?
quiz.explain: Colouring every other sector matches every 120°: 360 ÷ 120 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Picks opposite sectors (order 2)

quiz.q: A circle has 12 equal sectors with sectors 1, 5 and 9 coloured. What is the smallest angle of symmetry?
quiz.explain: The coloured sectors are 4 apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.
quiz.mistake: Uses one sector's angle

quiz.q: A 2 × 2 tile design has two plain tiles on the left and two tiles with vertical stripes on the right. How many lines of symmetry?
quiz.explain: Only the horizontal middle line works; left and right differ.
steps: Left tiles are plain, right tiles are striped, so a vertical fold does not match.
Top and bottom rows are the same, so the horizontal middle fold matches.
quiz.mistake: Counts the vertical line too

quiz.q: A 2 × 2 design has plain tiles at top-left and bottom-right, and tiles with vertical stripes at the other two corners. Which turn keeps it the same?
quiz.explain: A half turn swaps top-left with bottom-right and top-right with bottom-left, keeping the pattern.
steps: A half turn (180°) swaps top-left with bottom-right and top-right with bottom-left.
Top-left and bottom-right are both plain; the other two are both striped.
So the design looks the same after 180° (a 90° turn would put stripes in plain places).
quiz.mistake: Thinks a quarter turn works

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can I turn a circle by any angle and it still looks the same?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Yes! Any turn about the centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry!
teach.nudge: Is there any turn that changes how a circle looks?

revise.summary: A circle looks the same after any turn about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry. Colouring sectors changes the order of rotational symmetry, and tile designs can be arranged to get chosen lines of symmetry.
focus: Know a circle's line and rotational symmetry
Find the order of a circle with coloured sectors
Check each fold line of a tile design
remember: Circle: same after a turn of any angle; every diameter is a line of symmetry
8 sectors, every other one coloured: order 4
8 sectors, two opposite coloured (1 and 5): order 2; one coloured: order 1
traps: A circle has endlessly many lines of symmetry, not 4
Colouring half the sectors does not always give order 2
Two coloured opposite parts give order 2, not 4

learn.hook: Two players, one grid, dominoes. Copy your opponent the clever way and you can't lose!
points: Game: on a grid, players take turns covering two neighbouring squares (a domino). The player who cannot move loses.
Symmetry strategy: on a 4 × 4 grid, the second player answers each move with the move you get by a half turn (180°) about the centre of the grid.
The copied squares are always empty, because the grid looks the same after a half turn, and no domino on a 4 × 4 grid can be its own copy. So the second player always has a move and wins.
Figures can have line symmetry only (letter A), rotational symmetry only (letter S, letter N), both (letter H, a square) or neither (letter F).

example.q: On a 4 × 4 grid, the first player covers the first two squares of the top row (top-left corner). Where should the second player play?
steps: A half turn about the centre sends the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.
So copy the domino onto the last two squares of the bottom row (bottom-right corner).
Keep copying like this after every move.
example.answer: The last two squares of the bottom row

learn.reallife: Chess and carrom players also use symmetry ideas to plan clever replies.

The board is symmetric before each move, and a domino never overlaps its own half-turn copy, so the copy squares are empty.
The letter S has rotational symmetry.
It looks the same after a half turn.
The letter A has rotational symmetry of order 2.
Upside down, A looks different.
A square has both line and rotational symmetry.

quiz.q: Which letter has rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry?
quiz.explain: S looks the same after a half turn but has no fold line.
steps: S looks the same after a half turn → rotational symmetry.
S has no fold line → no line symmetry.
A and E have line symmetry; H has both.
quiz.mistake: Thinks S has a line of symmetry

quiz.q: Which letter has both line and rotational symmetry?
quiz.explain: H has a vertical and a horizontal line and matches after 180°.
steps: H has a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry.
H also matches after a 180° turn.
A has no rotational symmetry; N has no line; F has neither.
quiz.mistake: Picks a letter with only one type

quiz.q: Which letter has neither line nor rotational symmetry?
quiz.explain: F has no fold line and doesn't match after any part turn.
steps: O and X have both kinds; Z matches after 180°.
F does not match after any part turn.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Z has no symmetry (it has rotation)

quiz.q: In the 4 × 4 domino game, the first player covers two squares in the top row, 2nd and 3rd from the left. Where does the half-turn copy go?
options: Bottom row, 2nd and 3rd from the left
quiz.explain: A half turn sends the top row to the bottom row, and the middle pair stays in the middle.
steps: A half turn sends the top row to the bottom row.
It also flips left and right: 2nd and 3rd from left become 3rd and 2nd.
So the copy covers the 2nd and 3rd squares of the bottom row.
Answer: Bottom row, 2nd and 3rd from the left
quiz.mistake: Copies across a line instead of turning

quiz.q: Why does the half-turn strategy always give the second player a move?
options: The board is symmetric after each pair of moves, so the copy squares are free
The first player always makes mistakes
quiz.explain: After every copy the covered squares are symmetric, so the half-turn copy of a new move lands on empty squares. A domino can never overlap its own copy, because the grid has no centre square.
steps: After each pair of moves the covered squares are symmetric under a half turn.
So the half-turn copy of any new move lands on empty squares.
A domino never overlaps its own copy, since a 4 × 4 grid has no centre square.
So the second player always has a move.
Answer: The board is symmetric after each pair of moves, so the copy squares are free
quiz.mistake: Does not see the role of symmetry

quiz.q: Who wins the 4 × 4 domino game if the second player uses the half-turn strategy?
quiz.explain: The second player always has a reply, so the first player runs out of moves first.
steps: With the half-turn strategy, the second player always has a reply.
So the first player is the one who runs out of moves.
The last to move wins, which is the second player.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the first player has the advantage

quiz.q: A shape has line symmetry but no rotational symmetry. Which could it be?
quiz.explain: A has a vertical line of symmetry but turned 180° it looks different.
steps: A circle and a square have both kinds of symmetry; S has only rotational.
The letter A has a vertical line of symmetry.
quiz.mistake: Thinks line symmetry always comes with rotation

quiz.q: What is the order of rotational symmetry of the letter N?
quiz.explain: N matches after 180° and 360°: order 2.
steps: Turn N by 180°: it looks the same.
Matches in a full turn: 180° and 360° → 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks N has no rotational symmetry

teach.praise: Tweet! Copy every move with a half turn about the centre. Gappu wins!
teach.nudge: How can you use the centre of the grid to answer each move?

revise.summary: In the domino game on a 4 × 4 grid, the second player always wins by copying each move with a half turn about the centre. Figures can have line symmetry only, rotational symmetry only, both, or neither.

learn.hook: What is colder than 0°C? What is below the ground floor? Welcome to the other side of zero!
points: Numbers less than zero are negative numbers: −1, −2, −3, ... We read −3 as 'negative three' or 'minus three'.
We use negative numbers for basement floors, temperatures below 0°C, depths below sea level and money we owe.
Zero is neither positive nor negative.
Every number has an opposite: +5 and −5 are the same distance from 0 on opposite sides. Together they make 0.
About 1400 years ago, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for working with negative numbers, which he called 'debts'.

example.q: It is 4°C at noon in Leh. By night the temperature falls by 7 degrees. What is the night temperature?
steps: Falling 4 degrees takes us from 4°C to 0°C.
We still need to fall 3 more degrees.

learn.reallife: Lift buttons show B1 or −1 for basements, and weather reports for Ladakh in winter use negative temperatures.

quiz.explain: −9 and 9 are the same distance from 0 on opposite sides. −9 + 9 = 0.
steps: Opposite numbers are the same distance from 0 on opposite sides.

steps: A debt is shown with a negative number.

steps: A negative number is less than zero.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero or a fraction is negative

quiz.q: Which number is neither positive nor negative?
quiz.explain: Zero sits between the positive and negative numbers, so it is neither.
steps: Positive numbers are right of 0; negative numbers are left of 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero is negative because it means 'nothing'

quiz.q: A submarine is 30 m below sea level (−30 m). A seagull flies 30 m above sea level (+30 m). How far apart are they?

quiz.mistake: Adds −30 and +30 to get 0, instead of finding the distance

teach.praise: Chirp! Negative numbers are on the other side of zero, like temperatures below freezing. Brrr!
teach.nudge: Where do these numbers sit compared with zero?

revise.summary: Numbers less than zero are negative numbers, used for basement floors, temperatures below 0°C, depths below sea level and money we owe. Every number has an opposite the same distance from 0, and zero is neither positive nor negative.
focus: Use negative numbers for floors, temperatures, depths and debts
Find the opposite of a number

remember: Negative numbers: −1, −2, −3, ...; −3 is read 'negative three' or 'minus three'

traps: −8 is colder (smaller) than −3, even though 8 is bigger than 3
Money owed is negative, not positive

learn.hook: The number line doesn't stop at zero. It stretches forever to the left too!
points: Integers are the whole numbers, their negatives and zero: ..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
On a number line, positive numbers are to the right of 0 and negative numbers are to the left.
A number further to the right is greater. So −2 > −5, and every positive number is greater than every negative number.
Moving right means going up (adding); moving left means going down (subtracting).
To find the distance between two numbers, count the steps between them on the number line.

example.q: Arrange −4, 3, 0, −7, 2 from smallest to largest.
steps: The negative numbers come first; the one furthest left is smallest: −7, then −4.

learn.reallife: Thermometers, lift panels and the scoreboard in some quiz games are number lines with negative numbers.

The distance from −4 to 4 on the number line is ___ units

quiz.q: Which is greater: −6 or −2?
quiz.explain: −2 is to the right of −6 on the number line, so −2 is greater.
steps: On a number line, numbers further right are greater.
quiz.mistake: Thinks −6 is greater because 6 is greater than 2

quiz.q: Which is the smallest of −3, 5, −10 and 0?
quiz.explain: −10 is furthest to the left on the number line, so it is the smallest.
steps: Order them on the number line: −10, −3, 0, 5.
quiz.mistake: Thinks −3 is smaller than −10

quiz.q: Riya starts at −4 on the number line and moves 6 steps to the right. Where does she land?
quiz.explain: 4 steps right takes her to 0, and 2 more steps take her to 2.
quiz.mistake: Moves left instead of right (−10)

quiz.q: How many integers lie strictly between −3 and 3?
quiz.explain: They are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. That is 5 integers. ('Strictly between' leaves out −3 and 3.)
quiz.mistake: Includes the end numbers (7) or forgets 0 (4)

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
quiz.explain: −7 is to the left of −1, so −7 is less than −1.
steps: −7 is to the left of −1, so −7 < −1 ✓.
−7 > −1 is false; 0 < −1 is false (0 is right of −1); −5 > 2 is false.
quiz.mistake: Compares the numbers without their minus signs

quiz.q: Arjun's building has floors from −3 (the lowest basement) up to 10. How many floors does the lift travel going from −3 to 10?
quiz.explain: From −3 up to 0 is 3 floors, and from 0 to 10 is 10 floors: 13 in all.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 10 − 3 = 7, ignoring that −3 is below zero

quiz.q: Which number is 5 steps to the left of 2 on the number line?
quiz.explain: 2 steps left reach 0, and 3 more steps reach −3.
quiz.mistake: Moves right instead of left (7)

quiz.q: One winter morning: Leh −6°C, Delhi 12°C, Srinagar −1°C, Manali 0°C. Which city is coldest?
quiz.explain: −6 is the smallest of these numbers, so Leh is the coldest.
steps: The smallest number is the coldest.
quiz.mistake: Picks Srinagar, thinking −1 is smaller than −6

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is −8 bigger than −2? Eight is bigger than two, right?'
teach.praise: Tweet! On the number line, further right is bigger. −2 is to the right of −8, so −2 is bigger!
teach.nudge: Where are −8 and −2 on the number line? Which way means bigger?

revise.summary: Integers are the whole numbers, their negatives and zero. On a number line, a number further to the right is greater, so every positive number is greater than every negative number.
focus: Compare and order integers using the number line
Move right (up) or left (down) on the number line
Count integers between two numbers and steps between them
remember: Further right is greater: −2 > −5
Every positive number is greater than every negative number
traps: Don't compare without the minus signs: −6 is less than −2
Between −3 and 3 there are 5 integers: don't include the ends or forget 0
From −3 to 10 is 13 floors, not 10 − 3 = 7

learn.hook: A magic lift has buttons +3 and −2 instead of floor numbers. Where will it take you?
points: Think of a lift button as a movement: +3 means go up 3 floors, −2 means go down 2 floors.
Starting floor + movement = target floor. From floor −2, pressing +5 takes you to floor 3.
To find which button to press, do target floor − starting floor. From floor 4 to floor −1: (−1) − 4 = −5, so press −5.
A positive movement goes up, a negative movement goes down, and 0 means you stay.

example.q: Meera is on floor 6. She wants floor −2. Which button should she press?

learn.reallife: Malls and hospitals often have basements B1, B2 (floors −1, −2), so lift trips cross zero all the time.

quiz.q: Rohan is on floor −1 and presses +4. Which floor does he reach?
steps: Start at floor −1; pressing +4 means go up 4.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the minus sign

quiz.q: Sana is on floor 3 and presses −5. Where does she go?
quiz.explain: 3 − 5 = −2, the second basement.
steps: Start at floor 3; pressing −5 means go down 5.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the wrong way

quiz.q: Which button takes you from floor 2 to floor −3?
quiz.mistake: Adds the floor numbers

quiz.q: Which button takes you from floor −4 to floor 2?
quiz.mistake: Uses 2 − 4

quiz.q: A lift moves −3 and reaches floor −1. Which floor did it start from?
quiz.explain: start + (−3) = −1, so start = −1 + 3 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding back

quiz.q: From floor −2, Ajay presses +3 and then −4. Where is he?
quiz.mistake: Makes a slip in one step

quiz.q: What movement takes you from floor −5 to floor −1?
quiz.explain: (−1) − (−5) = 4, so press +4 (go up 4 floors).
quiz.mistake: Thinks going to a negative floor is always down

quiz.q: Pressing which button keeps you on the same floor?
quiz.explain: A movement of 0 means no change.
steps: To stay on the same floor, the movement must be zero.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must move

teach.ask: Gappu is on floor −2 and wants floor 4. 'Which button do I press?'
teach.praise: Tweet! 4 − (−2) = 6, so press +6!
teach.nudge: How do you find the movement from the start to the target?

revise.summary: A lift button is a movement: +3 means up 3 floors and −2 means down 2 floors. Starting floor + movement = target floor, and the button to press is target floor − starting floor.
focus: Find the target floor from a start and a movement
Find the button to press as target − start
Work backwards to find the starting floor
remember: Starting floor + movement = target floor: −2 + 5 = 3
Button = target floor − starting floor: (−1) − 4 = −5
Positive goes up, negative goes down, 0 means stay
traps: Don't ignore the minus sign on a floor number
Going to a negative floor is not always down: −5 to −1 is +4
Don't add the floor numbers to find the button

learn.hook: A +1 token and a −1 token cancel out to make zero. With this one trick you can add any integers!
points: Token model: a positive token (+1) and a negative token (−1) make a zero pair. Remove zero pairs to find the answer.
Adding a positive number moves right on the number line; adding a negative number moves left.
Same signs: add the sizes and keep the sign. (−4) + (−3) = −7.
Different signs: subtract the smaller size from the bigger and use the sign of the bigger one. (−9) + 5 = −4.
Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8.

steps: (−6) + 9: 6 zero pairs cancel, leaving 3 positive tokens → 3

learn.reallife: Bank passbooks show deposits (+) and withdrawals (−), and board games move you forward and back.

games.title: Integer facts
items: A number and its opposite make zero.
Subtracting a negative number makes the answer bigger.
Subtracting −3 is the same as adding 3.
Both are negative, so the answer is −7.
Adding a negative number moves you left on the number line.
Adding −2 is like taking 2 steps left.
The sum of two negative integers is always negative.
Two debts together are a bigger debt.

quiz.explain: 3 positive tokens cancel 3 of the 7 negative tokens, leaving 4 negative: −4.
steps: The bigger size (7) is negative, so −4
quiz.mistake: Ignores the signs and adds (10) or gets the sign wrong (4)

quiz.explain: Both numbers are negative, so add the sizes and keep the minus sign: −14.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the sizes (−2 or 2) or drops the minus sign (14)

quiz.explain: Subtracting −4 is the same as adding 4: 9 + 4 = 13.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as 9 − 4 = 5

quiz.q: Aisha has ₹20 but owes her brother ₹35. If she pays back all she can, what is her money position?
quiz.explain: 20 + (−35) = −15. She still owes ₹15, so her position is −₹15.
steps: So her position is −₹15 (she still owes ₹15).
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the result is still a debt and writes ₹15

quiz.q: A diver is at −12 m (12 m below the surface). She swims up 5 m. Where is she now?
quiz.explain: Swimming up means adding: −12 + 5 = −7 m. She is 7 m below the surface.
quiz.mistake: Moves down instead of up (−17)

quiz.q: Which gives the same answer as 4 − (−6)?
quiz.explain: Subtracting −6 is the same as adding its opposite, +6. So 4 − (−6) = 4 + 6 = 10.
steps: Subtracting a number = adding its opposite.
quiz.mistake: Thinks subtracting a negative still means taking away

quiz.explain: Subtracting −5 is adding 5: −15 + 5 = −10.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as (−15) − 5 = −20

quiz.q: In a board game, Joseph moves +5 spaces, then −8 spaces, then +2 spaces. Where is he compared to the start?
quiz.explain: 5 + (−8) + 2 = −3 + 2 = −1. He is 1 space behind the start.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the minus sign and adds everything (15) or gets the sign wrong (1)

teach.ask: Gappu has 5 red (−1) tokens and 3 green (+1) tokens: 'What is (−5) + 3? How do I work it out?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! 3 zero pairs cancel out, and 2 red tokens are left: the answer is −2!
teach.nudge: What happens when a green token and a red token meet? And what is left over?

revise.summary: Integers can be added and subtracted using tokens or the number line. Same signs: add the sizes and keep the sign; different signs: subtract the sizes and use the sign of the bigger; subtracting a number is adding its opposite.
focus: Add integers with the same and different signs
Subtract by adding the opposite
Solve word problems with debts, depths and games
remember: Same signs: (−4) + (−3) = −7
Different signs: (−9) + 5 = −4
Subtracting a number = adding its opposite: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8
traps: Don't drop the minus sign: (−6) + (−8) = −14

topics.title: Mine levels and the unmarked number line

learn.hook: A mine lift goes 200 m underground. Big negative numbers, no problem!
points: Integers can be large: a mine has levels like −40 m, −120 m, −250 m below the ground (0).
Adding and subtracting large integers works just like small ones: (−120) + 75 = −45, and (−45) − 80 = −125.
An unmarked number line is a quick sketch: put 0 somewhere, draw a jump right for adding a positive and left for adding a negative, and label the landing points.
You don't need every mark: to find (−35) + 60, jump 35 right to reach 0, then 25 more to reach 25.

example.q: A miner at −150 m goes up 90 m and then down 40 m. Where is he?
steps: He is at −100 m (100 m below the ground).

learn.reallife: Coal mines in Jharkhand go hundreds of metres deep, and submarines dive to large negative depths too.

games.title: Mine levels from deepest to highest
items: 0 m (ground)

quiz.q: A mine lift is at −240 m. It rises 130 m. Where is it now?
steps: Start at −240 m; rising 130 m means add 130.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sizes and keeps the minus

quiz.q: A miner at −75 m goes down another 60 m. What is the new level?
steps: Start at −75 m; going down 60 m means subtract 60.
So the new level is −135 m.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the sizes

quiz.q: How far apart are the levels −40 m and −170 m?
steps: So they are 130 m apart (a distance is not negative).
quiz.mistake: Adds the two sizes

quiz.q: On an unmarked number line, how do you show (−30) + 50?
options: Start at −30, jump 50 to the right, land on 20
quiz.explain: Adding a positive moves right; 30 of the jump reaches 0 and 20 more lands on 20.
steps: Adding +50 means jump 50 to the right.
30 of the jump reaches 0; 20 more lands on 20.
Answer: Start at −30, jump 50 to the right, land on 20
quiz.mistake: Moves left for a positive

quiz.q: Use an unmarked number line: (−45) + 100 = ?
quiz.explain: Jump 45 to 0, then 55 more.
steps: Start at −45 and jump 100 to the right.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the wrong way

quiz.q: Use an unmarked number line: 60 − 110 = ?
quiz.explain: From 60, jump 60 left to 0, then 50 more left: −50.
steps: Start at 60 and jump 110 to the left.
quiz.mistake: Ignores crossing zero

quiz.q: A mine has levels at −80 m, −160 m and −240 m, equally spaced. What would the next level be?
quiz.explain: Each level is 80 m deeper: −240 − 80 = −320.
steps: So the next level is −320 m.
quiz.mistake: Adds 80 instead

quiz.q: A lift goes from −180 m to +20 m (a viewing tower above the mine). How far does it travel?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the sizes

teach.ask: Gappu's worm is at −90 cm in the soil and wriggles up 120 cm. 'Where is it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! 90 cm up reaches 0, then 30 more: it's at +30 cm, above ground!
teach.nudge: How far does the worm go to reach 0?

revise.summary: Large integers, like mine levels below ground, are added and subtracted just like small ones. An unmarked number line is a quick sketch with jumps right for positives and left for negatives.

Find the distance between two levels
Use an unmarked number line, jumping to 0 first
remember: (−35) + 60: jump 35 right to 0, then 25 more to 25
Adding a positive: jump right; adding a negative: jump left

learn.hook: Red tokens for +1, black tokens for −1. Put one of each together and… poof, zero!
points: A positive token stands for +1 and a negative token for −1. So 3 positive tokens show +3, and 4 negative tokens show −4.
A zero pair is one positive and one negative token together: (+1) + (−1) = 0.
To add, put the tokens together and remove zero pairs. (+5) + (−8): remove 5 zero pairs, 3 negative tokens remain, so the answer is −3.
To subtract, take tokens away. If there are not enough of the kind to remove, first add zero pairs (this doesn't change the value).
(−3) − (+2): take away 2 positives from 3 negatives? There are none, so add 2 zero pairs. Now remove the 2 positives: 5 negatives remain, so −5.

example.q: Use tokens to find 4 − (−3).
steps: There are no negatives to take away, so add 3 zero pairs.
Take away the 3 negatives: 7 positives remain. Answer: 7.

learn.reallife: Ancient Chinese mathematicians used red and black rods in a very similar way to tokens.

games.title: Token rules
items: A zero pair is worth 0.
+1 and −1 cancel.
Adding a zero pair changes the value.
It adds 0.
6 negative tokens and 2 positive tokens show −4.
2 zero pairs leave 4 negatives.
To work out 2 − 5 with tokens, you must add zero pairs first.
There are only 2 positives to take away 5.
Removing zero pairs makes the answer smaller.
It removes zeros only.

quiz.q: A bag has 7 positive tokens and 3 negative tokens. What integer does it show?
quiz.explain: 3 zero pairs cancel; 4 positives remain: +4.
steps: Pair each negative with a positive to make a zero pair.
3 zero pairs use 3 positives and 3 negatives.
quiz.mistake: Adds all tokens

quiz.q: What is (+2) + (−6) using tokens?
quiz.explain: 2 zero pairs cancel, leaving 4 negative tokens.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the signs

quiz.q: Using tokens, (−5) + (−2) = ?
quiz.explain: No zero pairs; 7 negatives in all.
steps: No positives, so no zero pairs.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the sizes

quiz.q: To find 3 − 5 with tokens, you start with 3 positives. What must you do first?
quiz.explain: You need 5 positives to remove, so add 2 zero pairs to get 5 positives.
steps: We must remove 5 positives but only have 3.
Adding 2 zero pairs adds 2 positives (and 2 negatives) without changing the value.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is impossible

quiz.q: After that, what is 3 − 5?
quiz.explain: Removing 5 positives leaves the 2 negatives from the zero pairs.
steps: Now we have 5 positives and 2 negatives.
quiz.mistake: Gives 2

quiz.q: Using tokens, (−4) − (−1) = ?
quiz.explain: Take 1 negative away from 4 negatives: 3 negatives remain.
quiz.mistake: Adds another negative

quiz.q: Using tokens, (−2) − (+3) = ?
quiz.explain: Add 3 zero pairs, then remove 3 positives: 2 + 3 = 5 negatives.
steps: Start with 2 negatives; we must remove 3 positives.
Add 3 zero pairs: now 3 positives and 5 negatives.
quiz.mistake: Removes negatives instead

quiz.q: Which collection of tokens shows 0?
quiz.explain: 4 zero pairs make 0.
steps: Zero needs every positive paired with a negative.
4 positives and 4 negatives make 4 zero pairs.
The other collections leave tokens unpaired.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any mix is 0

teach.ask: Gappu has 2 positive tokens and wants to take away 3 positive tokens. 'I don't have enough!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Add a zero pair, then take away 3 positives: you're left with −1!
teach.nudge: What can you add without changing the value?

revise.summary: A positive token is +1 and a negative token is −1, and one of each makes a zero pair. To add, combine tokens and remove zero pairs; to subtract, take tokens away, adding zero pairs first if needed.
focus: Read the integer shown by a set of tokens
Add using tokens and zero pairs
Subtract by first adding zero pairs when there aren't enough tokens
remember: Zero pair: (+1) + (−1) = 0
(+5) + (−8): remove 5 zero pairs, 3 negatives remain: −3
Adding zero pairs doesn't change the value

3 − 5 is not impossible: add 2 zero pairs, then remove 5 positives: −2
(−2) − (+3): remove positives (after adding zero pairs), not negatives

learn.hook: An 'amazing grid': circle one number in each row and column, and the total is always the same. Magic? No, maths!
points: Hollow square grid: numbers sit only on the border. The puzzle is to make all four sides add to the same sum. Corner numbers count for two sides.
To find a missing number, use the side whose other numbers are all known: side sum − known numbers = missing number.
Amazing grid: each entry is (row label) + (column label). Circle one number in each row and each column: you always use every row label and every column label once.
So the circled sum always equals (sum of row labels) + (sum of column labels).

example.q: A 3 × 3 grid has rows: (2, −5, 0), (5, −2, 3), (3, −4, 1). Circle 2, −2 and 1 (one in each row and column). What is the sum? Try another choice.

learn.reallife: Puzzle magazines love grids like these. They train you to add negative numbers quickly.

games.title: Grid facts
items: In a hollow grid, a corner number belongs to two sides.
It sits where two sides meet.
In the amazing grid, every valid choice gives the same sum.
It always uses every row and column label once.
Circling two numbers in the same row is allowed.
One per row and one per column.
The missing number = side sum − the other numbers on that side.
That's how to solve it.
Negative numbers can't appear in these grids.
Integers of any sign can.

quiz.q: A hollow grid side has −4, ?, 7 and the side sum must be 5. What is the missing number?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the negative sign

quiz.q: Another side has 7, −6, ? with sum 5. What is missing?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts −6 as if it were 6

quiz.q: A side has −3, ?, −3 with sum −10. What is missing?
quiz.mistake: Adds the sizes

quiz.q: In the grid rows (2, −5, 0), (5, −2, 3), (3, −4, 1), Ravi circles −5 (row 1), 3 (row 2) and 3 (row 3, column 1). What is the sum?
quiz.explain: −5 + 3 + 3 = 1. Same as always!

quiz.q: Why does the amazing grid always give the same sum?
options: Each choice uses every row label and every column label exactly once
quiz.explain: Each entry is row label + column label, and any choice includes all labels once.
steps: Each entry = its row label + its column label.
A valid choice takes one entry from each row and each column.
So it always adds every row label and every column label exactly once.
That is why the sum is always the same.
Answer: Each choice uses every row label and every column label exactly once
quiz.mistake: Thinks it works by luck

quiz.q: An amazing grid has row labels 3, −1 and column labels −2, 4. What is the sum of any valid choice of 2 numbers?
steps: Sum = all row labels + all column labels.
So any valid choice sums to 4.
quiz.mistake: Adds only the rows

quiz.explain: 1 is row 1 column 1; 3 is row 2 column 2: one per row and column. 1 + 3 = 4 ✓.
steps: A valid choice takes one number from each row and each column.
1 is in row 1, column 1; 3 is in row 2, column 2 → valid.
quiz.mistake: Picks two from the same row or column
